title: Manhunt for Massachusetts woman ends with grim discovery week after police officer husband found dead at home
summary: Police said preliminary evidence suggests Karen Solomon died by suicide after her body was found near a Worcester rehabilitation hospital, ending a dayslong search following her husband’s death.
story: Officials in Worcester, Massachusetts, said they believe a body found in the woods Monday by employees of a rehabilitation hospital is Karen Solomon, who was wanted in connection to the death of her husband, WPD Officer Kurt Solomon.

The body of a woman believed to be Karen Solomon, the missing wife of a veteran Worcester, Massachusetts, police officer found dead last week, was discovered in city woods Monday with a handgun nearby, authorities said.
Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said two Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital employees discovered the body while walking near the facility at about 12:40 p.m.

"Upon further examination, we believe this person to be Karen Solomon," Saucier said at a news conference, stressing that the identification is preliminary and still must be confirmed by the medical examiner.

Police said they believe Solomon died by suicide, Saucier said, adding that preliminary evidence showed she had a gunshot wound. Investigators recovered a handgun near her body, but Saucier said it was not a service weapon.
SPECIAL FORCES VET ACCUSED OF TRYING TO KILL WIFE FOUND DEAD, ENDING MASSIVE TENNESSEE MANHUNT
Karen Solomon, 58, was wanted by police in Massachusetts. (Worcester Police Department)
The department now believes the case was a "tragic murder-suicide," though the investigation remains ongoing, Saucier said.
Karen Solomon, 58, had been missing since her husband, Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon, was found dead inside the couple’s Wildwood Avenue home on Aug. 18.

Police responded to the residence at about 5:28 a.m. after receiving a report of a person down and found the off-duty Worcester police officer dead inside, authorities said. His cause and manner of death have not been released.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED POLICE OFFICER AND HIS GIRLFRIEND

Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. arrives at Westside Animal Clinic while law enforcement searches the Coes Pond area during the investigation involving Karen Solomon and the death of Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Authorities initially said Karen Solomon was a suspect they wanted to question about what happened at the home and warned that she was believed to be armed and dangerous.

The woman’s body was found about 0.6 miles from an area where police had released video showing Solomon walking behind an animal clinic, Saucier said. The Coes Pond area and park, which police had been searching since the first day of the investigation, spans about 90 acres.
Saucier said investigators cannot yet say when Solomon died. Police did not receive any reports of a gunshot being heard Monday, he said.

The chief also pushed back on speculation surrounding domestic violence. The case was described as domestic under Massachusetts law because it involved family or household members, he said, but added that the Solomon family had no history of domestic abuse.
The Solomon family said the "nightmare of the past week" had left them "heartbroken and rudderless" in a statement read by Saucier.

"The compassion, dedication and empathy of all the agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness," the family said, thanking local, state and federal law enforcement agencies that joined the search. "You have given us comfort knowing that you were working on our behalf for us."
SUSPECTS IN DEADLY CONNECTICUT HOME INVASION ARRESTED IN ATTACK THAT ROCKED BEACH TOWN

Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon, a 31-year department veteran who was identified by the New England Police Benevolent Association after an off-duty officer was found dead at a Worcester home. (The New England PBA, Inc.)
Police have disclosed few details about what happened inside the residence, citing the ongoing investigation.

Public records reviewed by The Associated Press show Kurt and Karen Solomon co-owned the Wildwood Avenue residence. Kurt Solomon also identified Karen Solomon as his wife in a 2016 bankruptcy filing, according to the AP.

The New England Police Benevolent Association identified Kurt Solomon as a 31-year veteran of the Worcester Police Department and remembered him as an "incredibly dependable officer, colleague and friend."

"Thirty-one years of service represents an extraordinary commitment to a community and to the profession of law enforcement," the association said. "Officer Kurt Solomon answered that call for more than three decades, and his service, friendship and dedication will not be forgotten."
The investigation remains ongoing.

story: Empire State Building climbers Ivan Kuznetsov and Angelina Nikolau return to a Manhattan court to face criminal charges over their engagement stunt. Prosecutors allege they broke a lock on a 104th-floor security door and entered restricted areas.

The newly-engaged couple, who police say scaled the Empire State Building last month, made their first court appearance on Monday in New York City and cameras were rolling as the couple appeared to make out as they exited the courthouse.

Ivan Kuznetsov, 32, and Angelina Nikolau, 33, were caught on camera kissing outside the courthouse following their NYC court appearance. (WNYW)

A 23-year-old pilot’s courage in safely ditching her twin-engine Piper in the Atlantic Ocean off Boca Raton, Fla., this weekend was matched by her calm humility in a statement thanking others rather than her own heroism.

"During the descent, my primary focus was ensuring the safety of everyone around me," Faith Tenkley, 23, said in a statement to Fox News. "I was able to navigate toward open water, successfully avoiding all nearby buildings, paddleboarders and swimmers (as well as individuals using metal detectors)."

Cleared by air traffic control (ATC) to land on a runway, her landing gear was malfunctioning, leaving her concerned about a hard landing with a plane still full of fuel.

A man suspected of killing five people in a rural area outside Portland, Oregon, was found dead inside a vehicle in Enumclaw, Washington, on Sunday in an apparent suicide, according to authorities.

Benjamin Charles Parker, 36, was identified as the suspect in a quintuple murder after the bodies of five dead people were discovered on Saturday at a home in a rural community near Forest Grove, Oregon, about 25 miles west of Portland.

"Through their investigation, they believed that Parker was in Enumclaw, WA. Officers from the Enumclaw Police Department located Parker’s vehicle and found him deceased inside. It is believed he died by suicide," the Washington County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

The sheriff's office previously said it responded early Saturday to reports of a vehicle fire at a property in Forest Grove, where the remains of five people and "several domestic animals" were discovered.

title: College grad reportedly dies in Six Flags roller coaster incident as family sues theme park
summary: Christopher Hawley, a recent San Diego State University graduate, reportedly collapsed after riding X2 in 2022, and his family now alleges the attraction was dangerously rough.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A California family reportedly filed a lawsuit accusing Six Flags Magic Mountain of a defective ride design after their 22-year-old son suffered fatal head trauma while riding the the X2 attraction.

The incident happened in summer 2022, when Christopher Hawley, a San Diego State University graduate, visited the Los Angeles County theme park with his family, according to Fox 11 Los Angeles. Hawley reportedly collapsed shortly after riding the X2 roller coaster and died the following day.
Separately, the X2 roller coaster was involved in another incident on July 5, 2026, when a rider was found unconscious, prompting the attraction to close for more than a month, KTLA reported.
Christopher’s death was ruled an accident caused by blunt-force head trauma sustained from the attraction, which his family described as exceptionally rough, Fox 11 said.
PANIC AT POPULAR THEME PARK AS STRANDED RIDERS SCRAMBLE TO ESCAPE BROKEN ROLLER COASTER
An aerial view of roller coasters at Six Flags Magic Mountain. Christopher Hawley, 22, reportedly suffered fatal injuries following a ride on the X2 roller coaster.  (Christopher Hawley/Facebook)
His younger brother, Alex, described the ride as intensely violent, saying it jerked passengers around before ending with a jolt that sent their heads slamming into the headrests.
"It was very rough. It just jerked us. It just jerked us all around," Alex told the local station.
"It just jolted us all the way forward and then our heads just swung all the way back into the headrest."
After Christopher stepped off the attraction, he reportedly appeared noticeably unwell, with his face turning very red before suddenly collapsing.
Emergency responders rushed him to a nearby hospital, but he succumbed to his injuries the next day, Fox 11 reported.
STARTLING FOOTAGE FROM AMUSEMENT PARK SHOWS THRILL RIDE HALTED AS GUESTS WAIT IN MIDAIR
The X2 ride, which allegedly caused Christopher Hawley to sustain fatal head trauma, features seats that rotate 360 degrees.   (Christopher Hawley/Facebook)

The family said a surgeon compared Hawley's injuries to shaken baby syndrome, a condition in which violent and sudden forces cause the brain to move rapidly within the skull, potentially resulting in swelling, bruising and bleeding.
"The surgeon had said, he likened it to shaken baby syndrome, that the ride hit his head so hard that it had basically ruptured his brain," Christopher's father, William, told the local station.
Six Flags declined to comment directly on the litigation to Fox News Digital.
However, the amusement park told Fox 11 that the ride remains closed following the separate July 2026 incident involving the unconscious rider.
"The ride remains closed at this time. It has been closed since the evening of July 12th," Six Flags said.
Christopher Hawley was a recent San Diego State University graduate when he died following a roller coaster ride. (Christopher Hawley/Facebook)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A jury trial involving Six Flags, the manufacturer of the X2 roller coaster and park employees is scheduled to begin Sept. 8, according to reports.
The lawsuit also alleges that the defendants failed to adequately warn the public about the ride's risks, the local station said.
X2 has been advertised as one of the theme park's most intense attractions and features seats that rotate 360 degrees.
The Los Angeles County Fire Department and the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: California dad paralyzed from neck down after diving into ocean to rescue child
summary: A California father dove into a rip current to save a child at a beach and suffered a spinal cord injury that left him paralyzed from the neck down.
story: Nathaniel Rai, 10, shares new details in an interview with Fox News Digital about his terrifying drowning experience and the remarkable friendship his family formed with the teen lifeguard who rescued him.
A California father of five was paralyzed from the neck down after entering the ocean in an effort to help a young child who his family said was caught in a rip current.

Josh Collette, 42, was spending time with his family at Riviera Beach in San Clemente, California, on Aug. 15, when a child believed to be 7- or 8-years-old became caught in a rip current, the man's sister, Hillary Collette, told KTLA.
The child’s mother first entered the water to go after her child, but Josh Collette ran past her and dove into the ocean in an effort to help the child, Hillary Collette told the outlet.
GEORGIA TEACHER, FATHER HAILED AS HERO AFTER DYING TO SAVE GIRL FROM MYRTLE BEACH RIP CURRENT
Josh Collette was paralyzed from the neck down after heroically diving into the ocean to help a young child who was caught in a rip current. (GoFundMe)
As he entered the water, Collette’s sister said he struck either a sandbar or rocks and was immediately injured.
Several people then rushed to his aid and helped pull him from the water. He told his wife right away that he believed he had broken his neck.
The child Josh Collette was attempting to help was safely pulled out of the water before Collette was brought from the water, his sister said.
Collette’s sister said doctors told the family that Josh Collette was paralyzed from the neck down.
Josh Collette inadvertently hit either a sandbar or rocks after entering the water, injuring him immediately. (GoFundMe)
His sister said he was unable to speak but communicated by moving his lips; she said the family expects him to regain his ability to speak.
His family created a GoFundMe as they prepare to help with medical bills, long-term therapy and support for the family as they navigate the long and difficult recovery ahead.

"Josh was hurt in an ocean accident on Sat Aug 15th he has a spinal cord injury," a family member wrote on the fundraiser. "The road ahead will be long, and the recovery will not be easy, we’re holding on to hope."
"We believe in miracles! We’ve already seen so many and thank everyone for the love, support, and prayers!" the fundraiser added. "Please keep praying for miracles! Its working!"
'HERO' FATHER DROWNS SAVING HIS 12-YEAR-OLD SON FROM RIP CURRENT AT POPULAR BEACH DESTINATION, FAMILY SAYS
Josh Collette with his wife and five children. (GoFundMe)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In an update shared on Friday, the family said it will take some time for him to no longer need medicine. The family also shared a picture of Josh Collette from his hospital bed.

"Yesterday was so positive and productive! So, it was hard to have a day with less progress. This guy hates medicine! He's trying hard to get off of everything... but, that's going to take some time. Thank you so much for all the prayers, love, and support. We love you all so much and feel so loved by all the help you’ve given us. We’re hanging in there and so grateful for all of you," the family wrote on the fundraiser.
The GoFundMe has raised nearly $110,000 as of Sunday night.

title: Minnesota tree trimmer charged in coworker’s death after on-the-job horseplay turns deadly
summary: A Minnesota tree-trimming employee faces a manslaughter charge after allegedly crushing his coworker’s head with a hydraulic grapple.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A tree-trimming employee has been charged with manslaughter after allegedly crushing his coworker’s head with a hydraulic grapple while the pair were reportedly "f—ing around" on the job, according to Minnesota authorities.

The incident happened in Apple Valley on Thursday when Christopher Boone Crimmins, 34, was operating machinery on the back of a truck while his coworker, Tyler Anthony Lynch, 26, was on the ground cleaning up branches, according to a criminal complaint filed by Dakota County.
Responding to reports of an incident, police discovered Lynch lying on the ground with "a significant amount of blood around him and significant trauma to his head," the complaint said.
Lynch was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the county.
WORKERS WARNED OHIO TRENCH WAS TOO DEEP BUT WERE TOLD TO ENTER MINUTES BEFORE FATAL CAVE-IN: REPORT
Christopher Crimmins has been accused of recklessly operating a boom when he allegedly killed his coworker. (Dakota County Jail )
Authorities said Crimmins was operating a boom, a movable mechanical arm attached to a truck, when he and Lynch began messing around with their shadows.
"He and the Victim were ‘f—ing around’ and saw that the sunlight was casting shadows of both the grapple and of the Victim on the street," the criminal complaint said.
While looking at the shadows, Crimmins allegedly maneuvered the grapple so that its shadow appeared to grab Lynch’s shadow.
However, he did not realize that the grapple itself was moving toward Lynch’s head.
TWO WORKERS KILLED, SEVERAL INJURED AFTER EXPLOSIONS TEAR THROUGH OHIO RECYCLING FACILITY

An employee operates a grapple to remove a tree from a residential property. A Minnesota tree-trimming worker was charged with second-degree manslaughter after allegedly crushing a coworker’s head with a hydraulic grapple while the two were horsing around with their shadows on the job. (Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images)
"Crimmins was not monitoring the actual grapple or Lynch. He then opened and closed the grapple, crushing Lynch’s head," the Dakota County Attorney's Office said.
A witness also saw the incident unfold and said the grapple appeared to "hit or pinch" Lynch’s head as it approached him.
WORKERS KILLED AND MANY TREATED AFTER REFINERY CHEMICAL RELEASE AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE CAUSE
Officers observed blood on the grapple, which was directly above Lynch, according to the complaint.

Authorities alleged Crimmins was responsible for the incident through negligence, saying he created an "unreasonable risk" and "consciously takes chances of causing death or great bodily harm to another."
A hydraulic grapple grips a large tree branch during a tree-trimming job. (Matthias Rietschel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Crimmins has been charged with one felony count of second-degree manslaughter. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine.

Officials said Crimmins was being held at the Dakota County Jail. Bail was set at $40,000 without conditions or $20,000 with conditions.

title: WATCH: Young bear takes rough tumble from Denver tree after wildlife officers tranquilize it
summary: Video captures a young black bear's rough tumble from a tree in Denver after Colorado Parks and Wildlife tranquilized it for relocation to better habitat.
story: The 100-pound bear was tranquilized and caught by officers before being relocated to better habitat (Credit: CPW NE Region).
A young black bear took a rough tumble from a tree in Denver on Sunday after wildlife officers tranquilized the animal before relocating it to a more suitable habitat.
Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said in a thread on X Sunday that officers responded to the bear near Louisiana Avenue and Pennsylvania Street in Denver.
"This morning we responded to a bear in a tree ... in Denver," the post read. "Not a typo. In Denver."
BEAR CAUGHT ON CAMERA PERCHED ATOP NEW MEXICO UTILITY POLE BEFORE REPORTEDLY SUFFERING FATAL ELECTROCUTION
A tranquilized black bear falls from a tree as Colorado Parks and Wildlife and Denver police respond in Denver on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)
Wildlife officers tranquilized the bear and worked with Denver Police Department officers to catch it as it fell from the tree, according to CPW.
"It didn't have the smoothest landing, but the bear is ok!" authorities said.
Video posted as part of the X thread showed the bear dropping through branches before officers secured the animal on the ground.
GATLINBURG POLICE FREE BLACK BEAR THAT LOCKED ITSELF INSIDE HOTEL BATHROOM IN WILD VIRAL VIDEO
A young black bear sits in a tree in Denver before Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers tranquilized and removed it on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)
CPW identified the animal as an approximately 1.5-year-old male yearling weighing about 100 pounds. The agency said the bear would be transported to better habitat and released.
The unusual Denver encounter comes as Colorado wildlife officials report an increase in bear activity this year, which they have linked to drought conditions and dwindling natural food sources.
CPW received 6,129 reports of bear sightings and conflicts between Jan. 1 and Aug. 13, compared with 3,115 during the same period last year, according to the agency.
BEAR CRASHES COUPLE'S ANNIVERSARY GETAWAY, RUMMAGES THROUGH TENNESSEE TEA SHOP BEFORE JUMPING ON COUNTER
A Colorado Parks and Wildlife officer prepares the tranquilized bear for transport after it was removed from a tree in Denver on Aug. 23, 2026. (Colorado Parks and Wildlife NE Region)
CPW also said in the X thread that drought conditions are driving more bears into neighborhoods in search of food.
"You're not crazy, we are seeing more bear conflicts this year," CPW wrote. "The drought is forcing bears to seek food in our neighborhoods."
Wildlife officials are urging Coloradans to secure their trash until the morning of pickup, remove bird feeders and keep cars and windows locked to prevent bears from finding food around homes.

The Denver encounter also came just days after a mother bear and cub wandered into the city's Harvey Park neighborhood. CPW tranquilized and relocated those animals after they remained in the populated area for several days.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Colorado Parks and Wildlife warns that bears can become increasingly active as they prepare for winter and search for enough calories to build their fat reserves.

title: American Airlines flight lands safely after laptop battery catches fire on board; passenger injured
summary: A passenger's laptop caught fire aboard American Airlines Flight 2398, filling the cabin with heavy smoke as crew used a thermal containment bag.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

An American Airlines flight landed safely in Dallas after a laptop battery caught fire on board, prompting flight attendants to contain the fire and emergency personnel to meet the aircraft, officials confirmed to Fox News Digital.

American Airlines Flight 2398 was approaching Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) on Friday after departing Atlanta when the crew reported a laptop battery fire, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
Flight attendants contained the fire with a thermal containment bag, the FAA said.
The Airbus A321 landed safely at DFW at about 6:55 p.m. local time, according to the agency. The FAA is investigating the incident.
TWO PLANES BLOW TIRES WHILE LANDING AT MAJOR US AIRPORT HOURS APART, FAA INVESTIGATING

An American Airlines Airbus A321 approaches San Diego International Airport on June 20, 2026. An American Airlines A321 landed safely at DFW on Aug. 21 after the crew reported a laptop battery fire on board. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
American Airlines separately confirmed to Fox News Digital that smoke was reported from a customer’s device during landing.

"American Airlines flight 2398 landed safely at DFW after reports of smoke from a customer’s device during landing. We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device," a spokesperson said.
The aircraft taxied to the gate under its own power, where emergency personnel met the plane in accordance with procedure, the airline said.

One passenger received medical attention at the scene and was released, the spokesperson said. DFW separately confirmed to Fox News Digital that emergency crews met the flight and one patient was treated and released.
FORMER NFL QB ROBERT GRIFFIN III DESCRIBES HARROWING ENGINE FIRE ON UNITED FLIGHT
A lithium-ion laptop battery is pictured in a stock image. The FAA says lithium batteries can pose a fire risk if they enter thermal runaway. (iStock)
The flight was carrying 133 people when the incident occurred, according to air traffic control audio obtained by CBS News.
Jessica Irgens, a passenger aboard the flight, told CBS News the fire began roughly 30 minutes before landing when another passenger’s laptop began smoking and caught fire.

Irgens said she was sitting two rows away and moved toward the back of the aircraft because of the heavy smoke. She told the outlet the laptop’s owner placed the device in the aisle and other passengers attempted to help.
The pilot reported to air traffic controllers that about four to five passengers may have suffered burns from the laptop, according to audio obtained by CBS News.
MULTIPLE INJURED AFTER FLOATPLANE MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING, CATCHES FIRE OFF WASHINGTON COAST

An American Airlines Boeing 737-800 sits at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Dallas, Texas, on Nov. 23, 2017. Officials confirmed one passenger was treated by medical personnel following the incident. (Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lithium batteries used in laptops, cellphones and other electronic devices can overheat through a process known as thermal runaway, according to the FAA.
The FAA said thermal runaway can occur without warning and can result from several factors, including a battery being damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged or improperly packed.

title: Georgia Walmart shopper picks up $30 from the floor, local police launch search for him
summary: The Albany Police Department's public search for a man who pocketed $30 inside a Walmart sparked widespread ridicule before the cash was returned.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Georgia man who pocketed $30 someone dropped on the floor inside a Walmart returned the cash after police publicly sought help identifying him, ending a case that drew ridicule from social media users who questioned why authorities were chasing a few lost bills.
The Albany Police Department in Georgia posted a photo of the man and asked the public to help identify him after another shopper dropped the cash at a local Walmart.
Police said the man picked up the $30 but did not turn it in to store employees.
CONSTRUCTION WORKERS UNCOVER $10 MILLION IN GOLD WHILE BUILDING SEWER UNDER FORMER BREWERY
Police in Albany, Georgia, launched a search for a man accused of picking up $30 from the floor in a local Walmart. (Albany Police Department)
The department’s post drew skeptical and sarcastic reactions from commenters who wondered whether the missing $30 called for a public search.
One user recalled finding a bank envelope containing $8,000 in a parking lot and said that was a different story.
"Now that is something you turn in, not $30 found inside a Walmart," the user wrote.
Another commenter imagined what might have happened if the money had been turned in to Walmart employees.
"ATTENTION SHOPPERS! $30 HAS BEEN FOUND. IF IT BELONGS TO YOU, PLEASE COME GET IT..." the user wrote.
Police said the incident happened at a Walmart at 2586 N. Slappey Blvd. in Albany, Georgia. (Google Maps)
"What's the crime lmao?" another user asked.
FLORIDA WOMAN ACCUSED OF HIDING THOUSANDS IN STOLEN CASH INSIDE BODY AFTER ALLEGEDLY SCAMMING SENIOR
The jokes even made their way to an unrelated police post about a shooting.

"I’m just thankful you guys captured that old man who found $30," one commenter wrote sarcastically. "I’m sleeping a bit more soundly knowing people aren’t out there just finding money like a bunch of savages."
Police later announced that the man had returned the money to its owner.
The victim initially wanted to pursue charges but changed their mind after getting the $30 back, according to the department.

Georgia law specifically addresses lost or mislaid property, making it a crime to knowingly keep such property without first taking reasonable steps to return it to its owner.

title: Uncontained brush fire in Nevada triggered by human activity; inferno grows to 13K acres
summary: Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency as the Hawk Fire exploded across 13,000 acres, threatening 1,000 homes outside of Reno.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The fast-moving brush fire that has scorched more than 13,000 acres outside Reno, Nevada, since erupting Saturday was caused by human activity, authorities said.
Firefighters have yet to contain any part of the blaze, which is threatening roughly 1,000 homes and has prompted evacuations for roughly 42,000 residents.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency for Washoe County as the Hawk Fire grew quickly throughout the day. Strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation helped fuel the flames, according to the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District.

About 400 firefighters and other personnel from local, state and federal agencies were working the fire Saturday night, both on the ground and from the air. Three helicopters were set to fly overnight as crews worked to protect homes and other property.
AI FIREFIGHTING DRONES TAKE AIM AT WILDFIRES
Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said the fire had already burned structures, though did not immediately specify what type of structures. (Facebook/Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District)
"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds," Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue Chief Richard Edwards said in a video posted to social media.
"The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas, creating a lot of challenges for our firefighters to save homes and protect lives," Edwards added.
Fire officials said the Hawk Fire burning outside Reno, Nevada, is threatening roughly 1,000 homes. (Facebook/Washoe County Sheriff's Office)
Officials ordered new evacuations for the Somersett community, including areas north of Somersett Parkway to Robb Drive, as well as neighborhoods north of West 7th Street to North McCarran Boulevard.
About 1,000 homes were also in a "Warning — GET SET" zone, with residents told to be ready to leave.
SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH
Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve urged anyone ordered to evacuate not to wait, saying the fire had already damaged structures.
Officials urged residents in evacuation zones to leave their homes. (Facebook/Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District)
"If you have been told to evacuate, please don't wait!" Schieve said in a statement. "Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building."

The mayor did not immediately specify what kind of structures were burned. She said leaving before the fire arrives also allows firefighters to focus on battling the flames rather than rescuing people who stayed behind.

The Hawk Fire exploded across more than 10,500 acres outside Reno on Saturday as strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation helped fuel the flames, officials said. (Facebook/Washoe County Sheriff's Office)
Lombardo also said the fire was threatening homes and other structures.
"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," the governor said in a statement.
Officials were also keeping a close eye on the fire near a Washoe County correctional facility.
Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said his office was working with fire and emergency crews and was prepared to act if conditions changed.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The safety and security of every incarcerated individual, as well as our staff, remains a top priority," Balaam said. "We will continue to evaluate conditions and respond accordingly."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Florida couple allegedly held four children in tractor-trailer cab for nearly seven years
summary: Four children were allegedly confined in a tractor-trailer cab for nearly seven years without school, showers or medical care in a Florida neglect case.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Florida couple is being charged with child neglect after allegedly keeping four children confined in the cab of a tractor-trailer for almost seven years without "time to take showers, use the restroom" or "exercise outside," arrest records show.
The children "have not been allowed to attend school for approximately five years," they told interviewers at a child advocacy center, according to an arrest report.

Keisha Epps, 51, and her fiancé, Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, have been living in the cab with the children while Epps works as a truck driver, driving a route between Miami and Atlanta, according to court documents.
Since December 2019, the children were kept inside the vehicle "for the majority of their days."
POLYGAMOUS SECT LEADER CONVICTED ON STATE CHARGES AFTER GIRLS FOUND IN UNVENTILATED TRAILER

A Florida couple faces four child neglect charges after investigators said four children spent nearly seven years largely confined inside a tractor-trailer cab. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images; Jacksonville Sheriff's Office)
A detective on the case reported the children were "walking with an unnatural gait from being confined to the cab."
They were "fed poorly," and they never received medical or dental care—even for emergencies, the report shows.
During the interview, one of the children recalled a time she "burned herself badly with cooked noodles."
"There was a lot of blood," she said.
Neither Stewart nor Epps took her to get medical treatment, the child told investigators. The child has a "permanent scar" from the burn, court records show.
16 CHILDREN FOUND LIVING IN 'DEPLORABLE' OHIO HOME CONDITIONS, 4 ARRESTED: 'PURE EVIL'
Court records say all four children shared a bunk so small they had to sleep curled up side by side inside the tractor-trailer cab. (Joe Raedle/Newsmakers via Getty Images)

Stewart "would watch" the children when Epps was sleeping, showering and driving the truck, the children said. And when the children witnessed sexual abuse and confronted Stewart, he "beat them by punching them in their heads," reports show. The identity of the alleged victim of sexual abuse wasn’t clear.
The children said they told Epps about the sexual abuse and saw her witness the sexual abuse. She called one "derogatory names and continued to leave them alone with" Stewart, reports show.
One of the children was found to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection.
All four children shared a bunk in the cab so small that they had to lie "curled up side by side because they could not fit," reports show.
ACTOR CHARGED WITH 24 FELONY COUNTS IN ALLEGED CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE CASE
Keisha Epps and Tamra Marshon Stewart were arrested Aug. 6 and remain jailed as they await trial on child neglect charges. (Jacksonville Sheriff's Office)
Both Epps and Stewart were arrested on Aug. 6, 2026, according to a heavily redacted report filed with the court by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office.

Epps and Stewart both were charged with four counts of child neglect—one count for each child. Each count of a third-degree felony is punishable by up to five years in prison, up to five years' probation and a fine of up to $5,000. Investigators said their actions demonstrated a "committed, willful failure or omission to provide a child with the care, supervision, and services necessary to maintain the child’s physical and mental health, including but not limited to, food, nutrition, clothing, shelter, supervision, medicine and medical services that a prudent person would consider essential to the wellbeing of the child."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

According to court documents, "capital sexual battery charges" against Stewart will be filed in the "9th Judicial District by the Statewide Prosecutor," a report shows. Under Florida law, anyone convicted of sexual battery of a child younger than 12 years old can face the death penalty or life in prison without parole.

All information about the children was redacted from reports, including their sexes, ages and relationships to each other and to Epps and Stewart. Epps and Stewart are being held in the Duval County Jail awaiting trial. Bond was set at $400,012 for Epps. Stewart was being held without bond.

title: Who's who? Meet the Penn State frat bros accused of operating the off-campus coke ring
summary: Fourteen suspects face charges in the alleged Penn State cocaine ring, with court documents revealing a hierarchy from suppliers to fraternity pledges.
story: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday and former acting DEA Administrator Derek Maltz weigh in on a large-scale cocaine trafficking operation at Penn State University. Authorities arrested fourteen individuals, including current and former students, for running a drug ring that used popular cash apps and Snapchat to distribute cocaine.

After news of the alleged Penn State fraternity coke ring broke earlier this week, individual complaints released by the Office of the Attorney General in Pennsylvania provide more specifics into each suspect's alleged involvement.

Those 14 complaints detail an alleged hierarchy within the cocaine-trafficking operation, from accused suppliers and distributors to fraternity members allegedly tasked with weighing, packaging and delivering cocaine.
Here are the suspects and their alleged roles.
All defendants are innocent until proven guilty.

Attorney General Dave Sunday announced that Agostino Abbatiello, 24, turned himself in Tuesday morning, was arraigned and denied bail. He is the accused Penn State coke kingpin. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
1. Agostino "Pablo Pledgescobar" Abbatiello
Alleged position: "Top of food chain" according to prosecutors.
Hometown: Westbury, New York
Age: 24
Major: Accounting
Fraternity: Sigma Chi
He reportedly made the dean's list at the university and "had a passion for numbers and financial storytelling," the New York Post reports. He is facing numerous felony charges.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Thomas Robinson, 22, is facing felony charges for his alleged involvement in the downstream logistics of the operation. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
2. Thomas Robinson
Alleged position: Downstream Logistics/Distribution
Hometown: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
Age: 22
Major: Human Resources and Management
Fraternity: Delta Upsilon

Robinson allegedly worked closely with Abbatiello and distributed cocaine from his frat to Penn State students, using Snapchat to sell to others. Detectives relied on confidential informants to bust the operation – an informant who purchased drugs from Robinson blew the operation open. He ultimately gave up his partner in crime – Abbatiello – once arrested.
MAN WANTED IN ROBBERY TIED TO PENN STATE STUDENT'S MURDER NOW SOUGHT AFTER OFF-DUTY COP SHOOTOUT
Mohammed Huraibi, 22, is facing felony charges in the alleged cocaine distribution ring. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
3. Mohammed Huraibi
Alleged position: Early distributor
Hometown: Secaucus, New Jersey
Age: 22
Major: Accounting/Finance
Fraternity: Delta Upsilon

According to court documents, he introduced Robinson to Abbatiello. Hurabi and Robinson initially split the cost on bulk cocaine purchases before Hurabi attempted to buy out of the partnership in late 2023. Despite stepping back from the bulk operation, he allegedly continued selling drugs to someone at another fraternity
JEANINE PIRRO CALLS OUT 'DIRTBAGS' AFTER 14 CHARGED IN ALLEGED COCAINE RING OPERATING FEET FROM A SCHOOLYARD
Lars Zeepvat, 24, is accused of sourcing the drug and transporting it in the operation. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
4. Lars Zeepvat
Alleged position: Business partner to Abbatiello and distributor
Hometown: Mendham, New Jersey
Age: 24
Major: Accounting
Fraternity: Sigma Chi

title: Bear crashes couple's anniversary getaway, rummages through Tennessee tea shop before jumping on counter
summary: Video captures a black bear jumping onto the counter of a Gatlinburg tea shop while a couple visiting the town for their anniversary trip stood feet away.
story: A couple visiting Gatlinburg for their seventh anniversary recalled the surreal moment a young bear wandered into a store, rummaged through tea and jumped onto the counter just feet away from them.

A couple's anniversary getaway took a wild turn when a bear strolled into a Gatlinburg tea shop and began rummaging through merchandise before suddenly jumping onto the counter in a startling encounter caught on video.

The couple, Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card, were visiting Gatlinburg to celebrate their seventh anniversary when they stopped at The Spice & Tea Exchange on Friday, which is where Card spotted an unexpected visitor near the entrance.
"There's a bear," Card recalled saying.
At first, Puyol said she didn't quite process what was happening, but when Card and the store clerk repeated themselves, she turned and saw the animal standing in the doorway.
HIDDEN DANGER AT POPULAR US NATIONAL PARK FORCES TRAIL CLOSURES AS BEAR SIGHTINGS CLIMB
Joshua Card first spotted the bear standing near the entrance of the tea shop before the animal ventured farther inside. (Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card)

The couple recalled guidance to back away from bears, but as they stepped away, the bear ventured farther into the store. The clerk directed them behind the register, where they had access to an emergency exit.

The curious intruder appeared particularly interested in the shop's inventory, tearing into a sweet-tea blend and investigating tea diffusers as a crowd gathered outside. An employee from a neighboring store sounded an air horn, the couple said, but it appeared to have little effect on the bear.
Card began recording as the bear approached the counter.
"Hey, what you doing there, buddy?" Card can be heard saying in the video.
BLACK BEARS INVADE LAKE TAHOE HOMES AS BREAK-INS SURGE AND LOCALS FORTIFY DEFENSES
A bear suddenly jumped onto the counter inside a Gatlinburg tea shop as Joshua Card recorded the unusual encounter. (Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card)
The bear then turned and jumped onto the counter, prompting Card to step backward.
"He's talking to this thing like it's a puppy," Puyol recalled. "It's a bear. It's not a puppy. It's a bear."
Card said he initially thought the animal might have been a "show bear" on a leash with a handler nearby because they were in such a populated area. He quickly realized it was a wild bear.

Card, a military veteran who also has experience as a lifeguard, said his background dealing with emergency situations helped shape his reaction. He described feeling uncertain about what the young animal was capable of and whether he should intervene or simply give it space.
"This didn't really feel like an emergency," Card said. "It felt unpredictable to me."
BEAR CUBS SPAR ON WOMAN'S FRONT PORCH IN ADORABLE VIRAL NATURE VIDEO, REACTIONS POUR IN
Card said the bear appeared more curious than aggressive.
"He didn't really seem threatened," he said. "Even when he jumped up on the counter, I was like, okay, well, I'm going to take a step back."
Puyol said she was more shocked than frightened.
"I wasn't scared," she said. "I was just shocked."
"I wasn't like, 'Oh my God, it's a bear, I'm going to die,'" she continued. "No, it was like, there's a wild animal, like eight feet away from me."
Adding to the irony, Puyol said she had repeatedly told Card before the trip that she hoped to see a bear during their anniversary getaway.
"Be careful what you wish for because I wanted to see a bear, not that up close and personal," she said.
WOMAN STALKED BY CHARGING BEAR ON MORNING DOG WALK CAPTURES TERRIFYING ENCOUNTER ON CAMERA
A bear wandered into The Spice & Tea Exchange of Gatlinburg while Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card were shopping during their seventh-anniversary getaway. (Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card)

The clerk eventually told the couple about another exit through the second floor, but the bear suddenly ran out before they needed to use it. Card and the clerk then shut the door and waited to make sure it was safe before leaving.
Puyol estimated the entire encounter lasted roughly 10 to 15 minutes.
The couple said store employees told them the bear appeared to be a repeat visitor and had entered the business earlier in the week.
The shop also posted a photo of a bear earlier in the week with the caption, "This young bear came into our shop today, snagged some sugar and came back for more!"
Now that they made it out safely, the couple said the encounter made for an anniversary they will never forget.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A bear wandered through a Gatlinburg tea shop, rummaged through merchandise and jumped onto the counter during an encounter caught on video by a couple celebrating their anniversary. (Victoria Puyol and Joshua Card)
"The trip has been filled with oddities, and so this just kind of ... fuels that whole experience," Card said.
Fox News Digital has reached out to The Spice & Tea Exchange of Gatlinburg for additional information.

title: Police make arrest after gunfire during California high school football game leaves 1 dead
summary: A 15-year-old was arrested on suspicion of murder and gang participation after a 17-year-old was fatally shot at a Bakersfield, California, stadium.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 15-year-old boy has been arrested in connection to a gang-related shooting that left a 17-year-old dead during a high school football game in Bakersfield, California, authorities told Fox News Digital.
The shooting happened shortly after 8 p.m. Friday at Independence High School as the school hosted Centennial High School for its season opener, according to the Bakersfield Police Department.
Neither the suspect nor the victim attended Independence High School, police confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Police said that while the shooting was not directly related to the football game, it happened while the game was underway. The shooting occurred within the exterior fence of the football stadium, but outside the chain-link barrier surrounding the field and track.
CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATION SHOOTING KILLS TEEN, INJURES CHILD AND TWO OTHERS

Independence High School in Bakersfield, California. Police said a deadly shooting occurred within the exterior fence of the school's football stadium while a game was underway Friday night. (Google Maps)
Officers found the 17-year-old suffering from gunshot wounds. He was taken to Kern Medical, where he was pronounced dead.
Authorities have not publicly identified the victim.
Police announced the arrest of the 15-year-old suspect Saturday on suspicion of murder, firearm-related offenses and participating in a criminal street gang, police told Fox News Digital.
POLICE ANNOUNCE ARREST AFTER 5 WOUNDED IN VIRGINIA STATE UNIVERSITY SHOOTING: REPORT
Deputies from the Kern County Sheriff’s Office responded to the campus after reports of gunfire.
Investigators said the suspect and victim knew one another and that the shooting "was not a random act of violence."

Police said a fight involving several people happened before the shooting. The gunfire erupted while the game was underway, sending players and spectators from the area, according to reports from the scene.
The game was canceled following the shooting.
Police told Fox News Digital that the gun used in the shooting has not been recovered. Investigators do not believe there are any additional suspects outstanding.
FEDS DISMANTLE ALLEGED GUN TRAFFICKING RING THAT FUNNELED DOZENS OF FIREARMS FROM GEORGIA TO CHICAGO GANGS
Officers from the Kern High School District, Bakersfield Police Department and Kern County Sheriff’s Office responded to the campus after reports of gunfire.

"Our deepest sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the 17-year-old who tragically lost his life. We also recognize the impact this incident will have on the family of the 15-year-old who was arrested," the Bakersfield Police Department said.
"Two young lives and two families have been forever changed by an act of violence, and we extend our compassion to everyone affected by this tragedy."
STUDENTS' PRE-PROM GATHERING TURNS INTO DEADLY NIGHTMARE AS BULLETS FLY

Independence High School in Bakersfield, California, where a 17-year-old was shot and killed during a football game on Aug. 21, 2026. Police said neither the victim nor the 15-year-old suspect attended the school. (Google Maps)

Kern High School District Superintendent Dr. Michael Zulfa said Independence High School staff and members of the district police department responded immediately after the shooting to protect students and spectators, and assist law enforcement and emergency personnel.

The school district said it is working with law enforcement as the investigation continues and will review the circumstances surrounding the shooting, Zulfa said. Counseling and other support services will also be available to students and staff.

"Friday night should have been an evening of school spirit, friendship, and community—a time for students and families to come together and celebrate the beginning of a new school year. Instead, an act of violence forever changed the lives of those who were there and has deeply affected our entire District," Zulfa said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The investigation remains ongoing.
Fox News Digital also reached out to the Kern County District Attorney's Office for additional information but did not immediately receive a response.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Syria off US terror blacklist after nearly 50 years as Trump admin clears investment hurdle
summary: The United States formally removed Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list after Marco Rubio authorized the rescission and delisted HTS.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The United States on Monday formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move Secretary of State Marco Rubio said eliminates the final major barriers to investment and economic recovery in the country.
Rubio said in a statement that he had authorized the formal rescission after a mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.
President Donald Trump had initiated the countdown in July after confirming to Congress that Syria’s government had ceased supporting acts of international terrorism.
"I have also delisted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT)," Rubio said Monday.
FORMER ASSAD-ERA PRISON CHIEF CONVICTED OF TORTURE IN US FEDERAL COURT, MARKING A HISTORIC FIRST

Syria’s president secured a major diplomatic boost as the U.S. removed the country from its terrorism blacklist, clearing key barriers to investment. (BING GUAN/POOL/AFP via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The actions, he said, represent "another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity."
Rubio said Washington had taken unprecedented steps over the past year to provide sanctions relief to the Syrian people.

He pointed to Trump’s June 2025 executive order, "Providing for the Revocation of Syria Sanctions," which accelerated sanctions relief by terminating the Syria Sanctions Program and the national emergency with respect to Syria while directing reviews of other Syria-related sanctions and terrorist designations.

"These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," Rubio said of the Syrian government.

Al-Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 in an offensive led by HTS rebels. Syria had been on the State Sponsors of Terrorism list since 1979, with the designation in force throughout al-Assad’s rule.
BRIEF ALCOHOL BAN IN DAMASCUS SPARKS CONCERNS ABOUT PRESIDENT AL-SHARAA'S VISION FOR SYRIA

Secretary of State Marco Rubio shakes hands with then Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel, on the sidelines of the 80th United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations headquarters, Monday, Sept. 22, 2025. (Bing Guan/Pool Photo via AP)

"In the past year, the Government of Syria has taken significant steps to counterterrorism, to include formally joining the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS in November and conducting operations to disrupt the terror networks of ISIS, al-Qa’ida, Hizballah, and Iran-aligned groups," Rubio said.

He added that rescinding Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism and HTS’ designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist "eliminates the final major barriers for private-sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy."
EVANGELICAL LEADER SAYS US MUST PROTECT SYRIAN CHRISTIANS FROM ATTACKS BY JIHADI TERRORISTS

Syrians gather in Umayyad Square, waving the Syrian revolution flags as they continue their celebrations after the overthrow of the 61-year Baathist regime and the end of the Assad family era in Damascus, Syria on Dec. 27, 2024. (Emin Sansar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Aug. 22 that lifting the designation would help restore Syria’s links to the global financial system and encourage investment following nearly 14 years of war.
"There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.

"Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said in a statement, adding that it is "in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria."

The governor of the Central Bank of Syria said Monday that lifting Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism is a "historic step that returns it to its natural place within the global economic system."
On Monday, Trump also posted a photo on Truth Social of al-Sharaa and al-Shibani holding his signed June 2025 executive order directing sanctions relief for Syria.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Putin ‘panicked’ as defiant Ukraine marks Independence Day under Russian bombardment
summary: Ukraine celebrated 35 years of independence amid fresh Russian attacks as an expert said Kyiv’s deep strikes and battlefield pressure have left Putin rattled.
story: Ukraine's Independence Day faced heightened security risks as former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, says Vladimir Putin is "panicked."

Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday under the shadow of continued Russian attacks, with one regional security expert arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "panicked" as Ukrainian forces strike deeper inside Russia.

The anniversary, commemorating Ukraine's Aug. 24, 1991, declaration of independence from the Soviet Union, came amid intensified Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure and heightened security concerns after Ukraine's Security Service warned of possible terrorist attacks ahead of the holiday.

European leaders joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv for Independence Day events in a show of support as the war grinds on. Zelenskyy declared that Ukraine wants peace but is not prepared to surrender to Moscow's demands.
A Russian drone strike Friday on a packed shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, killed at least 16 people and injured 130, according to The Associated Press.
'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)
Putin has warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian economic targets open a "Pandora’s box," while Kyiv maintains deep strikes are vital to disrupting Moscow’s logistics.
Ukraine has targeted Russian economic infrastructure, including warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.

"The war with Russia has seen a lot of advances for the Ukrainians over this year," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.
"They've recently been able to actually penetrate much deeper into Russian territory, including close to Moscow and St. Petersburg."

"Their success on the military front has now resulted in the Russians getting panicked and starting to attack more inside Ukraine and what they're really trying to do is weaken their will and capabilities," Filipetti said, adding that Putin "gets very anxious when he's put in a corner."

"What we're seeing is these sorts of gasps at trying to retain some kind of control," Filipetti added. "This is why he recently targeted a shopping mall inside Ukrainian territory. He is not focused on targeting military assets. He is really focused on trying to defeat the will of Ukrainians by attacking them."
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY
The anniversary came amid intensified Russian strikes. (REUTERS /Gleb Garanich)
Filipetti warned the targeting of civilian areas created heightened security risks as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day, more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.

Several European leaders traveled to Kyiv for Ukraine’s Independence Day events, including European Council President António Costa and leaders from Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Denmark, Estonia and Latvia.
Filipetti said the high-level participation underscored continued international support for Ukraine.
TRUMP'S TURKEY ARMS SALE PROPOSAL SPARKS CONGRESSIONAL QUESTIONS BEFORE NATO SUMMIT

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported. (HENRY NICHOLLS / Pool via REUTERS)

"Independence Day is a really important moment for the allies of the Ukrainians to really show that we are not losing steam, that we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty," Filipetti said. "But anytime there's massive public gatherings, particularly to demonstrate patriotism and support for the Ukrainian state, it increases the security risk."

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported.
"They should be particularly mindful about sharing any videos or photographs that could betray the locations of some of their frontline soldiers," Filipetti warned.
DRONE OFFENSIVE HITS RUSSIAN OIL TANKERS AND REFINERIES AT 'INDUSTRIAL SCALE' AS MOSCOW BANS DIESEL EXPORTS

Russian glide bombs strike food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia Rescuers work at the site of a reported strike on a food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on July 8, 2026.  (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Monday's holiday came after a lethal exchange of drone and missile strikes. Ukrainian officials reported at least seven deaths from Russian attacks, while a Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's Krasnodar region killed three, according to Russian officials, The Associated Press reported.

"The Russians really want to bleed the Ukrainians of people, equipment, and will before the Russians are bled of those same three things," Filipetti said. "And what we've seen over the course of this year is almost no territorial gains on behalf of the Russians."
They are losing more soldiers each month than they can recruit, forcing them to rely on North Korean, Cuban and other foreign fighters to fill the gap, Filipetti added.
ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR

President Vladimir Putin prioritizes Russia's nuclear triad strengthening as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns the Russian leader has launched "World War III." (Genya SAVILOV / AFP via Getty ImagesContributor / Getty Images)
"Remember, Putin thought that this was going to be a special military operation that was going to last a matter of weeks," Filipetti said.
Ultimately, she emphasized that Ukraine's resolve delivers a firm deterrent beyond Moscow.

"It sends a message to the Russians that any invasion of sovereign territory, like their invasion of Ukraine, is going to create more consequences for them," Filipetti said. "We are not losing steam, and we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty."
Filipetti said it also sends an important message to other American adversaries like China.

"These adversaries of the United States really learned from how the United States handles conflicts in other theaters. It's really important that our adversaries of China, Russia, Iran, and others understand that if they invade another country unilaterally, there are going to be consequences, not rewards."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Massive garbage heap collapses onto homes, killing at least 30 as rescuers search for survivors
summary: A mountain of garbage collapsed after heavy rain at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and launching a search for survivors.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
At least 30 people were killed in a massive landslide in Guinea on Sunday when a mountainous open-air landfill collapsed and buried nearby shacks, trapping numerous victims beneath a mass of garbage.
The incident happened at Dar Es Salam, the largest waste dump in the West African country's capital, Conakry, according to a report from The Associated Press (AP).
Guinea News reported that the weight of the waste caused a three-story building beneath it to cave in.
Authorities said heavy rainfall also washed over the refuse overnight, creating hazardous conditions at the landfill, according to the AP.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS
Residents and rescuers use an excavator to search for victims after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed in the incident, according to reports. Officials launched a search-and-rescue operation to find any survivors.

The AP reported that the landfill was originally scheduled to close Sunday after officials warned of hazardous conditions, citing Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion.
The decision followed reports of a similar incident at the landfill in recent years, raising concerns about its safety.
Thirty people were killed and six others seriously injured after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
As a precautionary measure, residents who lived near the site had also been given eviction notices and were forced to vacate the area, the AP said.
However, many people remained nearby at the time of the disaster, according to reports.

The Dar Es Salam landfill collapsed following heavy overnight rain in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
"We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere," Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene, according to the AP.
Reuters reported that the landfill suffered a similar incident in 2017, when torrential rains caused a mudslide that killed at least eight people.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
story: Mexican Senator Lilly Tellez discusses the indictment of a Sinaloa governor and nine officials for alleged fentanyl trafficking. She blasts President Claudia Sheinbaum's refusal to extradite, asserting Mexico operates as a 'narco-state.' Tellez warns of deep corruption and the dire implications for bilateral relations and border security.

Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him.
Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor.
The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again.
MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT

Sinaloa Gov. Ruben Rocha Moya speaks as he leaves the inauguration ceremony of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico City, Mexico, on Oct. 1, 2024. (Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027.
"Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X.
Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government.
He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions.

Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents.
MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED
"I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote.
Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open.

Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X.
"No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to Rocha's return to office on Saturday. (Daniel Cardenas/Getty Images)
"Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added.

U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States.
U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses linked to the Sinaloa cartel. (Solidago/Getty Images)
Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters.

title: Hormuz crisis hides a deeper oil threat that could outlast the war
summary: Art Berman warns that 8 million barrels shut in near the Strait of Hormuz may never fully recover, even after a ceasefire reopens the waterway.
story: Art Berman says millions of barrels of production remain shut in and warns some wells could take months to restart — while others may never fully recover.

As global attention remains fixed on tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a petroleum geologist is warning that the more consequential energy story may be unfolding thousands of feet underground — and could continue long after any political agreement ends the fighting.

Art Berman, a petroleum geologist and energy consultant with more than four decades of industry experience, told Fox News Digital that millions of barrels of Persian Gulf oil production remain shut in and warned that restoring those wells is far more complicated than simply reopening the strategic waterway.
"This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues," Berman said.

"The bigger story and the more important one long term is that 8 million barrels of Persian Gulf production is currently shut in and world production is down about 10 million barrels a day," Berman explained.

In an aerial view, Marathon Petroleum Corp's Los Angeles Refinery, one of the largest oil refineries in North America, operates as gas prices rocket upward due to worldwide oil supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran, on March 10, 2026 in Carson, California. (David McNew/Getty Images)

"We can move tankers around and we can obsess about, you know, are there 4 million barrels getting through or are there 6 million or 9 million or whatever the right number is," he added. "But eventually, those tankers have to be filled with oil."

A White House official, speaking on background, pointed to the sharp decline in oil prices following the signing of the MOU and said the Strait of Hormuz is open, with the U.S. naval blockade in full effect.

Berman's estimate of Gulf shut-ins is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the International Energy Agency. The IEA said in its Aug. 12, 2026, Oil Market Report, "Gulf oil production rose by a further 2.5 mb/d in July to 23.9 mb/d, still 8.3 mb/d below pre-war levels."
Global oil supply remained 6.3 million bpd below year-earlier levels, according to the agency.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration offers a somewhat different estimate.

EIA assessed production shut-ins at an average 5.5 million bpd in July, while warning that continuing constraints on Hormuz transit had forced the agency to increase its forecast for shut-in production in August. EIA expects production and trade patterns to generally return to pre-conflict conditions in early 2027, but says some Gulf producers may not regain their previous output during its forecast period.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on Aug. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

The distinction is important because much of the public discussion has centered on what the industry calls the midstream problem — whether tankers can safely transport oil through Hormuz — while Berman argues that the upstream problem of producing the oil itself could prove more enduring.
"The very last thing in the world I ever want to do is to shut in a well," Berman told Fox News Digital.

Restarting a well requires restoring communication between equipment at the surface and reservoirs thousands of feet underground, he explained, and extended shutdowns can create complications inside the reservoir and well.
"This is not like turning on a switch for a light bulb," Berman said. "It's a complicated, high-risk, relatively long-term process, and we don't know the outcome."

Berman estimated that roughly 80% of affected wells could return close to their previous production levels, although he said that could take weeks or months. He said many of the remainder could require additional engineering work and some could ultimately produce at lower rates.
"Some of that production will never come back," he predicted.
Other energy analysts agree that restarting Gulf production presents substantial technical challenges. But Wood Mackenzie is more optimistic than Berman about the ultimate recovery.

Its analysis projects that fields affected by the Hormuz closure could return to approximately 70% of their previous production within three months and 90% within six months, assuming a controlled restart. The final roughly 1 million bpd could take considerably longer.
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
Berman also warned against assuming that a ceasefire or political agreement would immediately restore pre-war energy flows.

Shipowners, insurers and crews would first have to become confident that tankers could safely navigate the waterway, while other logistical and security issues could continue even after governments reached an agreement.
"A simple political agreement doesn't mean the problem's over," Berman said.
Berman's argument goes considerably further than predicting a slow oil-market recovery.
He contends that the Persian Gulf conflict represents a fundamental shock to the global energy and economic system — one whose consequences will persist even after the immediate crisis ends.

Asked about his comparison with the COVID-19 pandemic, Berman told Fox News Digital that the scale of oil production affected by the current crisis makes it comparable to the largest economic disruptions of recent years.
"This is not just a news cycle," Berman said. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues."
IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING
The ConocoPhillips Oil Refinery is seen in Wilmington, California on April 11, 2026. (Etienne Laurent / AFP via Getty Images)
The United States is the world's largest oil producer, but Berman argues that does not isolate American consumers from the disruption.
"The oil market and the refined products market is global," he told Fox News Digital.

Berman noted that U.S. refineries require different grades of crude to produce the country's mix of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other petroleum products, meaning domestic production alone cannot eliminate America's exposure to international markets.
"The problem for the U.S. isn't that we don't have enough oil, we almost do," Berman said. "It's that the oil we have isn't the right kind" for everything American refineries produce.

EIA reported July 15 that Hormuz disruptions had already pushed international buyers toward alternative sources of petroleum products, contributing to higher U.S. refinery margins, production and exports.

Whether that recovery proceeds as EIA expects or encounters the technical obstacles Berman warns about could determine how long the economic consequences of the conflict linger after the shooting stops.
For Berman, the question is no longer simply when tankers return to Hormuz. It is whether the global energy system that emerges afterward will ever operate quite the way it did before.

The White House pushed back on concerns that the disruption represents a lasting threat to U.S. energy security, pointing to record American production and blaming Iran for instability in the critical shipping corridor.

"Thanks to President Trump, the United States is now the world’s number-one producer and exporter of oil and gas. Record oil and gas production strengthens our energy independence and national security," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

"The Iranian regime’s terrorist actions in the Strait of Hormuz have proven that our allies need to invest in reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources and advance new partnerships with the United States that enhance the world’s energy security," Rogers added.
Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026 off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. ( )
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, U.S. Energy Information Administration and Defense Intelligence Agency for comment.
