title: California attorney general cancels talks with Paramount, accuses company of leaks
summary: Paramount insisted it has “not been the source of the leaks” about confidential talks with California, which sued to block the company’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.
story: California’s attorney general called off a meeting Monday with Paramount Skydance to discuss a potential settlement of the state’s antitrust lawsuit seeking to block the media company’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
In a statement Monday morning, California Attorney General Rob Bonta confirmed he “pulled down this meeting” and accused Paramount of “playing games.”

“I prefer to resolve disputes in the boardroom, not the courtroom. As I’ve also said, if the opposing party in litigation wants to meet in good faith to make a sincere effort to resolve the case, we’ll meet,” Bonta said in part.

Bonta accused Paramount of leaking “the alleged substance of settlement discussions” that were held on Friday. “But they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the Democratic official added.
In response to a request for comment Monday, a spokesperson for Paramount said the company shared Bonta’s “concerns about the public discussions and misreporting that has surrounded this deal.”
“As we have assured the Attorney General’s office, Paramount has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office,” the Paramount spokesperson added.
Bonta and the Paramount spokesperson appeared to be referring to a Wall Street Journal article published Saturday that detailed some of the conversation topics at Friday’s meeting.
The back-and-forth is the latest twist in a corporate saga that has riveted Hollywood in recent months.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America filed a lawsuit last month challenging the tie-up between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of the country’s leading entertainment and media conglomerates.

The states contend the deal violates federal antitrust law and threatens to “extinguish” economic competition in three markets: wide-release theatrical films, anticipated top-grossing movies and basic cable television distribution.

Paramount has flatly rejected those claims, calling the states’ lawsuit “wrong on both the facts and the law.” It has argued that the merger will increase economic competition and production output across film and television.

The company has agreed to freeze the merger until either the antitrust challenge is resolved or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is presiding over the case, scheduled an antitrust trial for early March.
Paramount has already won clearance from the Department of Justice and secured regulatory go-aheads from more than 60 territories around the world, including Australia, China and the European Union.

The combined corporation would be led by David Ellison, the 43-year-old son of Oracle mogul Larry Ellison. It would encompass two movie studios, two streaming platforms, a suite of cable channels and two marquee news organizations: CBS News and CNN.

Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of its traditional headquarters in California unless Bonta opened settlement talks, according to a source who was in a closed-door meeting earlier this month but wasn’t authorized to speak about it on the record.

If the deal hasn’t closed by Oct. 1, according to the companies’ agreement, Paramount will be on the hook for a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. shareholders, or roughly $650 million a quarter.
California political leaders have urged both sides in the legal conflict to get to a resolution.

“The continued uncertainty is not good for the workers, not good for productions and not good for the future of this industry,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat running for re-election, said last week.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed concerns that the antitrust challenge could harm California employment if the deal is blocked.
In response to NBC News’ request for comment on that report, Newsom’s office said it “doesn’t comment on anonymous sources or unverified reporting.”

In the antitrust challenge, California is joined by the Democratic attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
story: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.
The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.
But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.
Add to Google
Add to Google

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.
Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.
“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.

title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
summary: For some in the predominantly Black city, the lack of electricity has caused medical complications, while others are cooking what food they can at local parks before it spoils.
story: GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.
Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.
“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”
Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.
“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.
As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.
Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”
Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”
“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.
Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.
“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.
Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.
“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”
On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.
“All gone, gone,” she said.
At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”
Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.
“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.
In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.
“It’s been crazy,” he said.
Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.
“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”
Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.
“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.
“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.
Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.
“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”
Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.
“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.
Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

title: Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into a key challenge for Sen. Darline Graham ahead of the South Carolina runoff.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into a key challenge for Sen. Darline Graham ahead of the South Carolina runoff. Plus, Allan Smith breaks down the shifting political landscape around data centers.
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
— Adam Wollner

⚖️ Breaking news: The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms. Read more →
Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — On Friday, a South Carolina Republican voter named Roger showed up to a Donald Trump and Darline Graham rally wearing a “DARK MAGA” T-shirt. He arrived early and waited hours to see the president speak.

But Trump’s endorsement wasn’t enough to convince him to vote for Graham in Tuesday’s high-stakes GOP runoff. Graham’s recent debate performance affected his perceptions after she said that “national security is not my thing” when asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are U.S. national security issues.
“Her people should have briefed her a little bit more,” he said. “Foreign policy is something that — you’re going to come in as a new senator, as a rookie, you’re gonna have to learn that.”
Glenda Clinkscales, who said she “loves Trump” and was “excited” to see him, didn’t harbor the same feelings for Graham. Like Roger, she was undecided.
“Some good answers and some not so good answers,” she said when asked what she made of Graham’s debate performance. “I’m not so sure about her right now.”
The hesitation by the two Trump supporters casts a cloud over Graham’s prospects for a six-year term as she faces five-term Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C.
Another voter, Daniel Musick of Myrtle Beach, labeled Trump “the best president we’ve ever had.” He had made up his mind for Norman even before watching Trump and Graham at the rally.

“It’s just that she’s untested. I don’t know enough about her,” he said, adding that “part of the reason” for his opposition to Graham is her debate moment. “Her answer on foreign affairs, when it came to China and Taiwan — it was really unclear that she knew her foreign policy, and to me that was the biggest issue.”

Norman has sought to capitalize on her debate blunder, but it’s not clear he is on the path to victory. Norman is 73, at a time when age is an issue for voters, and has been accused by Graham’s team of being insufficiently loyal to Trump as a member of the House Freedom Caucus that seeks to push his agenda to the right.
Graham, 62, has defended her debate moment by saying voters in South Carolina aren’t asking her about China and Taiwan.

“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at Friday’s rally with Trump. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”
Trump, for his part, said Graham was just “being honest” in the debate.
“I mean, she’s going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump told reporters Friday before the rally.
To other GOP voters who attended Friday’s event, Trump’s support was enough.
“Honestly, I don’t know as much about the platforms there, but if Trump supports her, I do too,” said Lynn Spivey, who was wearing a Darline Graham sticker.
Patrick Maguire contributed.
📱Related: MAGA Inc., the super PAC tied to Trump, has spent $830,000 on text messages and voter phone calls to boost Graham, Bridget Bowman reports.
Republicans wrestle with data center backlash as Trump promotes the benefits
As recently as last month, Republicans in some of this fall’s biggest races publicly expressed skepticism about the growing backlash to data center development.

A lot has changed since then. On Thursday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced support for a one-year moratorium on data center development. In Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Republican nominees for governor cut ads hitting their Democratic rivals for being too open to the projects.

Earlier this month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who had welcomed the developments to his state and faces re-election this fall, ordered an audit of data center projects in the state before any more can advance. And in Ohio, GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy released a plan stating that any future data center built in the state must pay the electricity bills and property taxes for nearby residents, adding that he will sign an executive order pausing development until such a plan is enacted into law.

Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote a memo last week for data center industry leaders detailing how in Ohio’s Senate race, the issue is single-handedly tearing down Republican Sen. Jon Husted as his Democratic rival, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, spends millions on anti-data center ads.

Data centers are one of the few issues in American politics that don’t fall along neat ideological lines. Both parties are rapidly trying to figure out what approach works best for them at the national, state and local levels. Democrats, including some who previously offered the industry a warm embrace, are similarly positioning to be seen as champions for data center accountability and tightly regulated growth as progressives angle for state and federal moratoriums on their development.

But the challenge is equally, if not more, daunting for Republicans, who have worked to build stronger relationships with tech leaders after they gravitated to President Donald Trump during his last presidential bid. And they’re campaigning as Trump himself has promoted the benefits of data center development needed to power the growth of AI.

“Following today’s SCOTUS ruling, California WILL SUE again to BLOCK Trump’s attack on mail-in voting!” Newsom said on X. “Every eligible voter gets a mail-in ballot here — and we’ll fight to keep it that way.”

His efforts to encourage Congress to pass his SAVE America Act legislation that would impose new voting restrictions nationwide, including proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter ID, have so far failed.

The Supreme Court decision is provisional, focusing only on the argument that U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani acted prematurely in preventing the provisions from being implemented in the 23 states before federal agencies had even drawn up plans for how to implement the executive order.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned ruling.

The decision leaves the door open to judges’ intervening later, especially with regard to any restrictions imposed for the coming midterm elections. On Friday, while the case was pending, the Postal Service issued its final regulation that would enforce parts of the executive order.
The dissenters were the three liberal justices on the conservative-majority court.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful. Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote.

In a separate dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson accused the majority of “taking its eye off the ball” by focusing on a technical legal argument instead of what she views as the larger goal of the Trump administration: “to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.”

The Trump administration told the Supreme Court the new regulations did not go as far as the executive order anticipated, saying the Postal Service “will not refuse to transmit ballots” even if senders are not on a state list of registered voters.

The Supreme Court decision is in line with one in a related case by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that rejected a separate attempt by Democrats to block the executive order.
Lower courts declined to put the Massachusetts ruling on hold, leading the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the filing that it was premature for courts to rule on the issue, as neither the Postal Service nor other agencies have determined how they will implement the executive order. It would be a tall order for the chronically underfunded Postal Service, with just months to go before Election Day.

title: Massachusetts woman wanted in police officer husband’s death believed to be dead
summary: Karen Solomon, a Massachusetts mental health advocate for law enforcement who was being sought in connection with the death of her police officer husband, appears to have been found dead Monday, ending a multiday search.
story: Karen Solomon, a Massachusetts mental health advocate for law enforcement who was being sought in connection with the death of her police officer husband, appears to have been found dead Monday, ending a multiday search.
Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier told reporters Monday that a body officials believed to be Solomon’s was found in a wooded area near a gun. Authorities are awaiting confirmation of her identity.

Investigators believe the deaths of Karen and Kurt Solomon, an officer with the department who was found dead on Aug. 18 at the couple’s home in Worcester, west of Boston, were the result of a murder-suicide, Saucier said.

In a statement read by Saucier, the Solomon family described the events of the last week as a “nightmare” that “has left our family heartbroken and rudderless. The compassion, dedication, and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”

“For those in Massachusetts and throughout the world who have offered up prayers and sympathies, they have helped us through each minute of the day,” the statement added. “Thank you for your basic human compassion.”

The search for Solomon began Tuesday after Kurt Solomon’s body was discovered. He was off duty at the time. Police had been called to the residence about 5:30 a.m. following a report of a person down.
Multiple agencies, including the U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations, assisted in the search. Saucier had said Karen Solomon should be considered armed and dangerous.

For years, she had advocated for the mental health of police officers and their families through First H.E.L.P., an organization she co-founded. She wrote two books. “Hearts Beneath the Badge” is about the experiences of law enforcement and their families, and “The Price They Pay” is about the emotional and physical effects of traumatic events on officers.

She also wrote articles about law enforcement suicide, according to a biography on her organization’s website, and participated in a 2020 Justice Department hearing of the President’s Commission on Law Enforcement and the Administration of Justice, where she testified on a panel focused on support for officers and their families.
Kurt Solomon was a patrol officer with the Worcester Police Department for more than 30 years and was nearing retirement, Worcester police union leader Thomas Duffy III said.

Authorities have not said how Kurt Solomon died, but they described his death as “an act of domestic violence.” Saucier said at Monday’s news conference that there was no history of domestic abuse in the family.

title: Former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges sexual assault on Disney Channel movie set
summary: In a lawsuit filed last week, Bolleau claims Disney ignored signs she was being sexually abused while on set of the 2001 film “The Poof Point.”
story: Former child actor Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges in a lawsuit filed last week that a male Disney employee sexually assaulted her while she was filming a network movie in 2001 and that the studio failed to respond to signs of abuse.
Bolleau was 14 at the time of the alleged attacks, which she said unfolded during the filming of the Disney Channel movie “The Poof Point.”
The plaintiff, now 39, said her alleged attacker, who is not named in the suit, was “a lifelong resident of California” who was more than twice as old as she was at the time.

“John Doe” was “an on-set, adult, middle-aged, male employee of Disney who was involved in the filming of the movie” who “repeatedly raped, sexually assaulted, sexually abused and sexually harassed” Bolleau, according to the suit, which was filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court on Friday.
“Mr. Doe’s sexual abuse of Ms. Bolleau was apparent to the adults on Disney’s set,” the suit states. “Disney repeatedly failed Ms. Bolleau.”
A representative of Disney, based in Burbank, California, could not be immediately reached for comment Monday.

Bolleau’s other credits include voicing Olei on Disney’s “The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder,” and Nubia Gross in “The Proud Family” original series and movie, according to IMDb. She has also appeared in shows like “Real Husbands of Hollywood” and films like “Stan the Man.”
She alleges the abuse she experienced derailed her career because she had “trauma of returning to a set,” according to the lawsuit.
Her lawsuit comes amid growing scrutiny of how child performers have been treated in Hollywood.

The 2024 documentary “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” detailed allegations of toxic working conditions on some Nickelodeon shows. Bolleau participated in the documentary, where she opened up about her experiences as a Black actor on “The Amanda Show,” but she did not discuss the allegations made in her recent lawsuit.
Other former child stars have since spoken about the pressures of growing up in the industry and called for stronger support.
Protections for child performers have expanded over the past decade, including new on-set advocates and tighter rules for adults working with minors.
But industry sources told NBC News last week that safeguards remain inconsistent and have not kept pace with growing awareness of the potential mental health effects of child stardom.
The alleged abuse toward Bolleau occurred in Utah, where “The Poof Point” was filmed, often in the man’s hotel room after he supplied her with alcohol, as well as on set, according to the lawsuit.

“On set, Mr. Doe regularly fondled and excessively touched Ms. Bolleau, often rubbing his genitals on Ms. Bolleau while giving her unsolicited hugs,” the suit states. “No one from Disney stopped this extremely inappropriate touching and molestation of a child.”
The abuse continued after the cast left Salt Lake City, with the man sexually assaulting Bolleau under a blanket as they flew back to California, the lawsuit said.
Bolleau’s work on “The Poof Point” suffered due to the alcohol and sex, according to the lawsuit.

“Disney recognized Ms. Bolleau’s sudden shift in demeanor and performance — clear indicia of child sexual abuse — and attacked, blamed and threatened Ms. Bolleau, a victim of rape, and Ms. Bolleau’s mother,” according to the lawsuit.
The studio “has been protecting and empowering sexual predators,” the lawsuit adds.
It’s unclear whether Bolleau or her guardian reported the 2001 assaults to the police.
The suit does not mention any police involvement. Bolleau’s legal team declined to comment on whether law enforcement had ever been notified.
Salt Lake City Police Detective Michael Ruff told NBC News in a statement Monday, “We do not have any records involving the name provided.”
“There over a dozen police departments in Salt Lake County, without further details it’s difficult to know if the accusations occurred within our jurisdiction,” Ruff said.
Bolleau’s lawsuit does not specify the amount of damages she is seeking.

“Over the last decade, countless child actors have come forward to bravely share their experiences of abuse by adults in entertainment,” Bolleau’s attorneys, Douglas Wigdor and Jane Kim, said in a statement, adding that those responsible “directly or indirectly” should be held accountable.

title: California attorney general cancels talks with Paramount, accuses company of leaks
summary: Paramount insisted it has “not been the source of the leaks” about confidential talks with California, which sued to block the company’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.
story: California’s attorney general called off a meeting Monday with Paramount Skydance to discuss a potential settlement of the state’s antitrust lawsuit seeking to block the media company’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
In a statement Monday morning, California Attorney General Rob Bonta confirmed he “pulled down this meeting” and accused Paramount of “playing games.”

“I prefer to resolve disputes in the boardroom, not the courtroom. As I’ve also said, if the opposing party in litigation wants to meet in good faith to make a sincere effort to resolve the case, we’ll meet,” Bonta said in part.

Bonta accused Paramount of leaking “the alleged substance of settlement discussions” that were held on Friday. “But they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the Democratic official added.
In response to a request for comment Monday, a spokesperson for Paramount said the company shared Bonta’s “concerns about the public discussions and misreporting that has surrounded this deal.”
“As we have assured the Attorney General’s office, Paramount has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office,” the Paramount spokesperson added.
Bonta and the Paramount spokesperson appeared to be referring to a Wall Street Journal article published Saturday that detailed some of the conversation topics at Friday’s meeting.
The back-and-forth is the latest twist in a corporate saga that has riveted Hollywood in recent months.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America filed a lawsuit last month challenging the tie-up between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of the country’s leading entertainment and media conglomerates.

The states contend the deal violates federal antitrust law and threatens to “extinguish” economic competition in three markets: wide-release theatrical films, anticipated top-grossing movies and basic cable television distribution.

Paramount has flatly rejected those claims, calling the states’ lawsuit “wrong on both the facts and the law.” It has argued that the merger will increase economic competition and production output across film and television.

The company has agreed to freeze the merger until either the antitrust challenge is resolved or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is presiding over the case, scheduled an antitrust trial for early March.
Paramount has already won clearance from the Department of Justice and secured regulatory go-aheads from more than 60 territories around the world, including Australia, China and the European Union.

The combined corporation would be led by David Ellison, the 43-year-old son of Oracle mogul Larry Ellison. It would encompass two movie studios, two streaming platforms, a suite of cable channels and two marquee news organizations: CBS News and CNN.

Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of its traditional headquarters in California unless Bonta opened settlement talks, according to a source who was in a closed-door meeting earlier this month but wasn’t authorized to speak about it on the record.

If the deal hasn’t closed by Oct. 1, according to the companies’ agreement, Paramount will be on the hook for a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. shareholders, or roughly $650 million a quarter.
California political leaders have urged both sides in the legal conflict to get to a resolution.

“The continued uncertainty is not good for the workers, not good for productions and not good for the future of this industry,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat running for re-election, said last week.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed concerns that the antitrust challenge could harm California employment if the deal is blocked.
In response to NBC News’ request for comment on that report, Newsom’s office said it “doesn’t comment on anonymous sources or unverified reporting.”

In the antitrust challenge, California is joined by the Democratic attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

title: Bessent threatens new Iran secondary sanctions, says Trump is asking world leaders to sign on
summary: Monday’s announcement was directed at countries whose trade and business relations still benefit the Islamic Republic.
story: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced plans for a wave of new sanctions Monday aimed at further isolating Iran, after threatening the Islamic Republic with “an economic D-Day.”
The sanctions will target international entities engaged in facilitating Iranian trade related to shipping, oil, crypto, gold and aviation.
Bessent said President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with “specific requests” to cease trading with the Iranian regime.

Bessent said the U.S. was launching an “economic onslaught” against Iran’s financial connections “around the globe” in order to “sever every economic pipeline” used by Iran “until Tehran stands alone.”

Treasury announced Monday it is sanctioning nearly 60 corporations, individuals and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that it says enable the Iranian regime’s “recklessness.” That list includes multiple Chinese nationals.
China has said it is illegal for its citizens to comply with unilateral U.S. sanctions.

Bessent said the U.S. was engaging in “quiet diplomacy” with Iranian trade partners to warn them of the consequences for continuing to trade with Tehran. Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the U.S. dollar system, he said.
“No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” Bessent said, adding there was now a “cure period” for nations to end the targeted relations with Iran.
Yet Bessent did not lay out any immediate concrete actions against other countries. Markets showed little reaction to Bessent’s remarks.
Iranian officials downplayed the economic threat.

“You will fail this time too,” Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said in response to Bessent’s comments, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency, and added, “The government is fully prepared for this economic war.”
Madanizadeh said that it would not be easy to cut the country off from global economic channels and that Iran would retaliate, according to the semiofficial ISNA news agency.
“If they take any action, they should expect an attack from us,” he said, according to ISNA.
Separately, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the U.S. must stop trying to bully Iran.

“America must correct its tone and approach in dealing with Iran, because relying on force and bullying will only complicate the process,” he said, according to the semiofficial Tasnim news agency. “Our nation, relying on its solidarity, will overcome any pressure and threats.”
Pezeshkian made the comments during a meeting on Monday with Field Marshal Asim Munir, the army chief of Pakistan, a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran, according to Tasnim.

After six months of kinetic combat and a U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Trump administration has few remaining levers it can use to convince Iran’s major trading partners to materially reduce their economic ties, said Alan Eyre, a distinguished diplomatic fellow at the Middle East Institute.
The White House “seems to think that this announcement in and of itself will cause countries to sever relations with Iran absent any follow-up, which I think is highly unlikely,” Eyre told NBC News.

The U.S. has for decades imposed direct sanctions on Iran and businesses involved in prohibited activities like weapons procurement. But Iran has, in many cases, successfully evaded the sanctions by setting up new front companies.
Bessent promised Sunday to launch “the single greatest financial offensive ever” in an op-ed in the Financial Times.

“The world should understand that our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” he wrote, adding that any country partnering with Iran would also be financially isolated.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Monday’s actions are designed to target “secondary” countries whose trade and business relations still benefit Iran. Ahead of the announcement, the United Arab Emirates, a close U.S. ally whose leadership has forged close ties with the Trump administration, announced it was ending all trade relations with Iran.
Experts say the success of Bessent’s announcement will hinge on whether Iran’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — decide the U.S. threats are credible.

“If you’re a country like Russia or China, you see Iran as ally, and you’re not just going to suddenly stop trading with them — that damages Moscow’s credibility in eyes of their friends around the world,” said Andrew Gawthrope, a university lecturer at the University of Leiden specializing in U.S. foreign policy.
“There’s just not much the U.S. can do to these countries to make them go along with this,” he said.
It’s been nearly six months since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on the premise of preventing it from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

The U.S. has racked up its own costs. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last month that the war has cost the U.S. $37.5 billion, though estimates put the all-in economic impact at as much as $150 billion. Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi told NBC News last month he estimated the war has cost the average U.S. household more than $1,200 in higher energy and grocery costs alone.
Despite the new economic measures announced Monday, Hegseth did not rule out further military action.

“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we’ll do what we need to do,” Hegseth told reporters Monday. “But economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now.”
“By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran.”

The war has also become a political liability for Trump ahead of November’s midterm elections, with his approval rating dropping to its lowest level of either of his presidential terms. Economists say that in addition to higher gas prices, the war has also helped contribute to the current turmoil in the bond market that’s led to extraordinary intervention by the Treasury Department.
While Bessent was speaking Monday, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament who until recently had been leading Iran’s negotiation team to end the war, took to X.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” he wrote. “Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere.”
Ahead of the speech, the country’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also posted on X to question whether Bessent’s plan was “an admission of America’s defeat?”

Referencing previous American claims that Iran’s military capabilities had been destroyed, he said, “Dealing with this very Iran has required the ‘largest financial offensive in history’ and the mobilization of ‘all of America’s institutions and authorities.’”

The head of Iran’s Central Bank, Abdolnaser Hemmati, told the semiofficial Tasnim news agency that the U.S. had “done everything it could in terms of sanctions up to now and the recent claims do not introduce any new restrictions or additional pressure.”
Iran had been anticipating “difficult conditions” since the war began in February “and began stockpiling foreign currency,” he said in comments that were published ahead of Bessent’s announcement.
This had enabled the country “to give a firm commitment that we would provide the foreign currency needed for essential goods and medicine,” he said.

In Tehran’s sprawling Grand Bazaar, long a center of conservatism in Iranian politics and still an economic force within the country, there was a heavy police presence and some expressed frustration at the value of Iran’s currency, the rial.
With gas prices on the rise and long lines reported at some gas stations, authorities in the country appeared concerned that protests could break out.

Violent demonstrations left thousands dead in January and thousands were arrested by the country’s hard-line regime after people took to the streets to call for an end to the country’s theocratic rule.

While President Donald Trump hoped for people to rise up against the country’s hard-line rulers early on in the war, Iran’s authoritarian government appears to have tightened its grip on power since the start of the war.

Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war along with several other senior officials. Now, his son and successor Mojtaba Khamenei appears to be equally hard-line, as he has elevated a group of veteran hard-liners from the country’s security and military establishment.

title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
story: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.
The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.
But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.
Add to Google
Add to Google

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.
Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.
“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.

It’s like giving your under-eye area a little massage.”

How I picked the best hands-free skin care
To come up with a list of the best hands-free skin care products, I asked experts for their top picks and for what to prioritize when shopping. Here is what the suggest:

So I prioritized formulas that have either been tested and vetted by NBC Selected editors, previously recommended by dermatologists and other experts, or come from brands with a proven record or efficacy and high shopper satisfaction.
Is it bad to use your hands to apply your skin care?

According to dermatologists, the answer is more nuanced than “hands bad, tools good.” As long as you’re using clean fingers, applying skin care with your hands isn’t actually a problem. “They are a perfectly appropriate applicator and give you good control over how much product you use and where it goes,” says Dr. Shamsa Kanwal, a board-certified dermatologist and consultant at the beauty hub My Psoriasis Team.

The real issue isn’t your skin — it’s what happens to the product. “The concern is introducing microorganisms into the product itself, particularly if you repeatedly dip unwashed fingers into a jar — this can introduce bacteria,” Kanwal says. In other words, washing your hands before you touch your face (or your jar of cleansing balm) matters more than avoiding your fingers altogether.
Are there any downsides to using hands-free skin care products?

Hands-free doesn’t automatically mean germ-free. “Hands-free formulas can be convenient and  less messy, but I would not assume they are automatically more hygienic,” says Kanwal. “Rollerballs and applicator tips repeatedly touch the skin and sprays can make it harder to judge whether you have applied enough product evenly.”
Frequently asked questions

If you’re team fingers, dermatologists say the fix is simple: wash up first. “I recommend washing and drying your hands before starting your routine, especially before applying products near the eyes or to irritated or compromised skin,” says Kanwal. “For products in jars, avoid repeatedly dipping dirty or wet fingers into the container, and use a clean spatula if one is provided.” That last step is an easy one to skip, but it can make a real difference in keeping bacteria out of your products in the first place.

Hands-free skin care refers to products designed with built-in applicators — think rollerballs, brush tips, sponge daubers and sprays — that let you apply the formula without ever touching it with your fingers. Instead of dipping into a jar or squeezing product into your palm, you roll, dab or mist it directly onto your skin. The category includes eye creams, serums, sunscreens, mists and more, and has grown popular among people looking for a cleaner, mess-free routine, even if, as dermatologists note, it’s not necessarily more hygienic by default.

title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
summary: For some in the predominantly Black city, the lack of electricity has caused medical complications, while others are cooking what food they can at local parks before it spoils.
story: GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.
Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.
“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”
Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.
“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.
As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.
Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”
Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”
“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.
Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.
“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.
Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.
“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”
On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.
“All gone, gone,” she said.
At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”
Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.
“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.
In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.
“It’s been crazy,” he said.
Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.
“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”
Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.
“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.
“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.
Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.
“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”
Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.
“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.
Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

title: Former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges sexual assault on Disney Channel movie set
summary: In a lawsuit filed last week, Bolleau claims Disney ignored signs she was being sexually abused while on set of the 2001 film “The Poof Point.”
story: Former child actor Raquel Lee Bolleau alleges in a lawsuit filed last week that a male Disney employee sexually assaulted her while she was filming a network movie in 2001 and that the studio failed to respond to signs of abuse.
Bolleau was 14 at the time of the alleged attacks, which she said unfolded during the filming of the Disney Channel movie “The Poof Point.”
The plaintiff, now 39, said her alleged attacker, who is not named in the suit, was “a lifelong resident of California” who was more than twice as old as she was at the time.

“John Doe” was “an on-set, adult, middle-aged, male employee of Disney who was involved in the filming of the movie” who “repeatedly raped, sexually assaulted, sexually abused and sexually harassed” Bolleau, according to the suit, which was filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court on Friday.
“Mr. Doe’s sexual abuse of Ms. Bolleau was apparent to the adults on Disney’s set,” the suit states. “Disney repeatedly failed Ms. Bolleau.”
A representative of Disney, based in Burbank, California, could not be immediately reached for comment Monday.

Bolleau’s other credits include voicing Olei on Disney’s “The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder,” and Nubia Gross in “The Proud Family” original series and movie, according to IMDb. She has also appeared in shows like “Real Husbands of Hollywood” and films like “Stan the Man.”
She alleges the abuse she experienced derailed her career because she had “trauma of returning to a set,” according to the lawsuit.
Her lawsuit comes amid growing scrutiny of how child performers have been treated in Hollywood.

The 2024 documentary “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” detailed allegations of toxic working conditions on some Nickelodeon shows. Bolleau participated in the documentary, where she opened up about her experiences as a Black actor on “The Amanda Show,” but she did not discuss the allegations made in her recent lawsuit.
Other former child stars have since spoken about the pressures of growing up in the industry and called for stronger support.
Protections for child performers have expanded over the past decade, including new on-set advocates and tighter rules for adults working with minors.
But industry sources told NBC News last week that safeguards remain inconsistent and have not kept pace with growing awareness of the potential mental health effects of child stardom.
The alleged abuse toward Bolleau occurred in Utah, where “The Poof Point” was filmed, often in the man’s hotel room after he supplied her with alcohol, as well as on set, according to the lawsuit.

“On set, Mr. Doe regularly fondled and excessively touched Ms. Bolleau, often rubbing his genitals on Ms. Bolleau while giving her unsolicited hugs,” the suit states. “No one from Disney stopped this extremely inappropriate touching and molestation of a child.”
The abuse continued after the cast left Salt Lake City, with the man sexually assaulting Bolleau under a blanket as they flew back to California, the lawsuit said.
Bolleau’s work on “The Poof Point” suffered due to the alcohol and sex, according to the lawsuit.

“Disney recognized Ms. Bolleau’s sudden shift in demeanor and performance — clear indicia of child sexual abuse — and attacked, blamed and threatened Ms. Bolleau, a victim of rape, and Ms. Bolleau’s mother,” according to the lawsuit.
The studio “has been protecting and empowering sexual predators,” the lawsuit adds.
It’s unclear whether Bolleau or her guardian reported the 2001 assaults to the police.
The suit does not mention any police involvement. Bolleau’s legal team declined to comment on whether law enforcement had ever been notified.
Salt Lake City Police Detective Michael Ruff told NBC News in a statement Monday, “We do not have any records involving the name provided.”
“There over a dozen police departments in Salt Lake County, without further details it’s difficult to know if the accusations occurred within our jurisdiction,” Ruff said.
Bolleau’s lawsuit does not specify the amount of damages she is seeking.

“Over the last decade, countless child actors have come forward to bravely share their experiences of abuse by adults in entertainment,” Bolleau’s attorneys, Douglas Wigdor and Jane Kim, said in a statement, adding that those responsible “directly or indirectly” should be held accountable.

title: 5 people and multiple animals killed on rural Oregon property, with suspect found dead
summary: A suspect in the killings of five people whose bodies, and those of several animals, were found on a rural property in Oregon was identified as one of the victims’ boyfriend, officials said.
story: A suspect in the killings of five people whose bodies, and those of several animals, were found on a rural property in Oregon was identified as one of the victims’ boyfriend, officials said.

The Washington County Sheriff’s Office identified Benjamin Charles Parker, 36, as the suspect in the “complex investigation.” On Monday, it identified one of the victims, 26-year-old Stella Kimsey, as his girlfriend.

Stella Kimsey’s mother, Rowan Kimsey, 60, and grandmother, Mary Kimsey, 85, were also identified among the victims. Her friend, Linsey Haraldsen, 26, and Haraldsen’s boyfriend, Alvin Chu, 27, were also killed, the sheriff’s office said.
On Sunday, the sheriff’s office said the Enumclaw Police Department found Parker dead in his car. “It is believed he died by suicide,” it said.
Enumclaw is a small city in Washington state.
Officials initially responded Saturday morning to a 911 call about a vehicle fire in unincorporated Washington County, outside the city of Forest Grove.
Washington County Sheriff’s detective Shannon Wilde said the “large scene” was on a rural property with some other homes around, and “a lot of vegetation.”
“I will say that in my 22 years here, I have not been a part of or witnessed a scene quite this complex involving this type of an investigation,” Washington County Sheriff Caprice Massey said.
Rowan Kimsey owned the property and lived there with Stella Kimsey and Parker, the suspect, the sheriff’s office said Monday.

Two cats and two dogs were found dead on the property, and a third cat was found injured and later euthanized due to the extent of its injuries, according to the office. Livestock on the property has been rehomed, it said.
There is no continued threat to the public, according to the sheriff’s office.
Forest Grove is about 25 miles west of Portland, Oregon, and 190 miles southwest of Enumclaw.

title: Father of sailor aboard USS Lincoln detained by immigration authorities, family says
summary: Joshua Aviles said he has been “fighting for a country that has given me everything,” only to learn his father had been detained.
story: The immigrant father of a sailor on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln was anxiously awaiting his son’s return home when immigration authorities detained him over the weekend.
Luis Manuel Aviles was taken into custody late Saturday morning near a Publix supermarket in Key West, Florida, where he lives, as he was headed to a mechanic, according to three family members.
“He was excited because he was finally going to be able to hug his son,” his wife, who requested her name not be published, told Noticias Telemundo on Sunday.
A Navy official confirmed to NBC News on Monday that their son, Joshua Aviles, who is a handling airman, is currently assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln.
The 25-year-old has been deployed inside the aircraft carrier for nine months, which is considered a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea.
Aviles’ wife said the father “was very happy, counting the days and weeks until his son arrived so he could hug him. And then, this happened.”

Originally from Nicaragua, Aviles has been living in the U.S. for 20 years, mostly working as a handyman for hotels in Key West alongside a string of other jobs to provide for his family, according to his youngest son, Luisito Aviles, and stepdaughter, Katty Delgado.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Sunday that Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles during a traffic stop in Key West. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.
“We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said.
In an interview with Noticias Telemundo on Sunday, Luisito Aviles described his father as the person who’s taught him everything he knows, from electrical issues to how to be a strong person.

“He never hid, he always did things the right way,” Luisito Aviles said in Spanish, adding that his father was working toward getting legal status and had complied with his paperwork and visits to ICE’s offices.
Delgado told NBC News on Saturday evening that she has no knowledge of an arrest history or criminal allegations against Luis Manuel Aviles.
“He’s doing everything the right way,” she said.
Delgado said that she learned the news from family members, including Aviles’ wife and his son Joshua Aviles, who posted a note about the detention on Facebook.

Joshua Aviles wrote on Facebook on Saturday, “I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything.”
He said that his father is hard-working, giving and humble and that he has a work permit, a Social Security card and a driver’s license.
“This is heartbreaking for me,” Joshua Aviles said. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.”

Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS told NBC News and Telemundo, NBCUniversal’s Spanish-language network, that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego on Nov. 25, and, with more than eight months since it visited a port in December, it broke the Navy record for time without a port call. Relatives of sailors on board the carrier have described reports of deteriorating conditions and morale. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about the situation on board have been “completely misrepresented.”
The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln has officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.
Joshua Aviles, who told NBC News he has limited internet access, wrote on Facebook that he’s doing everything he can to get his father released from detention.
“I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad,” he wrote.

President Donald Trump has stood by his administration’s immigration crackdown, including ICE’s expanded enforcement and arrests, which in recent months have included the arrests of children and spouses of service members, a San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator and a grandmother from India who’s a schoolteacher with a green card.

Immigration authorities have detained more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during Trump’s second term, according to a recent Associated Press investigation. There has been backlash to the detentions, which come despite programs for military members that can sometimes offer immediate family protection from deportation.
The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website says those “discretionary options” are offered on a “case-by-case basis.”
It was not immediately clear whether Luis Manuel Aviles was in the program.
The DHS spokesperson said in a statement Sunday that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.”
“Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the spokesperson said.
Delgado lamented that her stepbrother has spent nine months out at sea, without seeing his family, “and this is what his father gets.”

title: ‘DWTS: The Next Pro’ Reveals Final 3 After Shocking Elimination
summary: Fans are just one episode away from learning which new pro is joining Season 35 this fall. Find out who was eliminated in the semifinals of “DWTS: The Next Pro.”
story: “Dancing With the Stars” fans are just one episode away from learning which new pro is joining Season 35 this fall.

At the end of the latest episode of the summer spinoff series, “Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro,” the three finalists were revealed. Judges Mark and Shirley Ballas, as well as guest judge and former pro Kym Johnson, announced the top three after the season’s most shocking elimination.

Episode 7 began with the remaining dancers — Adele Zaikman, AJ Pritchard, Allen Genkin and Selena Hamilton — learning that for the semifinals they would have to choreograph and perform two routines that wowed the judges, just like the pros are asked to do on “DWTS.”
“You’ve all proved you’re great dancers, but now we need to dig deep. To decide whether you have the choreography, the teaching skills and the personality,” Shirley explained.
For their first dance, the contestants were paired with four current pros on the show, creating the following duos:
Adele and Gleb Savchenko dancing the sambaAJ and Rylee Arnold dancing the cha chaAllen and Witney Carson dancing the jiveSerena and Jan Ravnik dancing the salsa
Adele and Gleb Savchenko dancing the samba
AJ and Rylee Arnold dancing the cha cha
Allen and Witney Carson dancing the jive
Serena and Jan Ravnik dancing the salsa
Then, the contestants teamed up with each other for their second dances of the night.
With the best dancers left in the competition, the margin for error was slim. See who impressed the judges enough to earn a spot in the finale.
What Happened During the ‘DWTS: The Next Pro’ Semifinals?

The first couple to dance was Allen and Witney. Before the performance, Witney mentioned in her feedback during rehearsals that Allen needed to work on his confidence. While he seemed to be the ideal leading man as they danced together, Shirley had some criticisms. She said the two were excellent when they were side by side, but she said Allen’s choreography didn’t highlight enough “wow moments” for Witney. Kym agreed with the critique, although she said the routine included many classic jive moves. Mark disagreed, however, and said it was his favorite jive of the season and he was bouncing in his seat the entire time.

Selena and Jan, who both have backgrounds as commercial dancers, were up next with their steamy salsa. Mark said Selena “nailed the brief” and he could see her routine being performed on “Latin Night” on “DWTS.” Kym called Selena a “star” and applauded her “clever” choreography. Shirley continued to praise her, pointing out Selena’s impressive balance and her chemistry with Jan.

Ahead of taking the dance floor, Adele revealed she was panicking a little and worried she wouldn’t be able to keep up with Gleb. But as soon as the music started, those fears seemed to dissipate. Kym said Adele was a great teacher and that her routine could appear on “DWTS.” Mark compared her fierce dancing to the movements of a “hooded cobra” ready to strike at any moment. Shirley called Adele and Gleb a “power couple,” but reminded Adele that she needs to include more “wow moments” that play to the cameras.

AJ, who has repeatedly shared in past episodes how long he has wanted to be a pro, had an intense rehearsal with Rylee. She expressed concerns about how his teaching style would work with a celebrity on “DWTS.” However, the two earned positive comments from the judges. Shirley said AJ went outside of his comfort zone and showcased Rylee well. Kym said AJ and Rylee’s personalities shined in the dance. But Mark, again, had a slightly different opinion. He said he wanted more “soul and funk and grit” in the routine.
For the second half of the episode, Adele was partnered with AJ for a foxtrot, and Selena and Allen were given the quickstep.

Close friends Allen and Selena danced together first. After the performance, Shirley said “the hardest thing to teach is a personality, and you both shine like bright lights when it comes to that.” Kym said she was most impressed by their creativity and musicality. Mark said the routine had “intention” and he enjoyed how much charisma they exuded.

The final dance of the night was performed by AJ and Adele. Even host Robert Irwin had to compliment the cool routine. Mark said the performance was “gorgeous.” Kym mentioned the chemistry between AJ and Adele and said the dance was “perfection.” Shirley, who constantly gave AJ tough criticism at the start of the competition, called him a “star.” As for Adele, Shirley said she is “the new generation for ‘Dancing With the Stars.’”
Who Was Eliminated on Episode 7, the Semifinals, of ‘DWTS: The Next Pro’?
Shirley gave each contestant a compliment before sharing how difficult it was to eliminate one person.
Since there were only four dancers, Shirley opted to just announce the name of the person going home instead of revealing a bottom two.
Shirley said there was one dancer who “ever-so-slightly underperformed.” She announced that Allen had danced for the last time on the show.

Allen said in his last confessional that he was “sad and devastated” to be going home. He added he had a great time and that he hoped he made his late mother proud. Robert told Allen that he connected with Allen’s story and passion. In his final words, Allen said he hoped his time on the show inspired viewers to pursue their dreams.
What Will Happen in the Finale?
Next week, “DWTS: The Next Pro” comes to an end with an epic finale airing on Monday, Aug. 31.

The teaser showed Mark and Shirley dancing together and a live audience joining the ballroom. Plus, each finalist will be paired with three “DWTS” alums: Adam Rippon, Nēv Schulman and Charli D’Amelio.
Who will win and appear on “DWTS” Season 35? Tune in to find out.

title: Fiona Dourif Is Thinking of Her Late Mom Amid First Emmy Nomination — And Her ‘Pitt’ Character’s Season 3 Story
summary: Fiona Dourif, who plays Dr. Cassie McKay in “The Pitt,” is up for best supporting actress at the Sept. 14 Emmy Awards.
story: The scene that made Fiona Dourif’s heart race the most on set for “The Pitt” Season 2 wasn’t simulating CPR or resetting a tailbone.
It was asking someone out.

In Episode 4, Dr. Cassie McKay gets dealt a flirty patient. After she diagnoses him with a non-fracture foot injury and permits his discharge, she confirms she won’t be seeing him again — “as a patient.” She starts to walk away, before doubling back and telling him she might check out an art gallery after her shift, around 9 p.m. He smiles.

“When I was actually shooting it, I remember my heart was beating out of my chest,” Dourif tells TODAY.com. “I’m somebody who has spent decades of my life single, and I know how scary that is. I’m actually quite bad at it. I’ve done it a couple times, but just the fear of rejection is really acute in the way that feels like a trauma bay.
“It’s also — it’s a funny thing when you play someone so close to my actual personality,” she adds. “I get nervous in places that I wouldn’t in my life and it just feels very exposing.”

Tapping into that raw nerve to play McKay, a resident in her 40s who made bad decisions growing up before deciding to turn her life around, has earned Dourif her first Emmy nomination, for best supporting actress in a drama series.

McKay is a third-year resident at the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center, known for an intuitive empathy inspired by her own traumatic past. She has a known experience with addiction but is now a sober single mom who started medical school in her 30s.

“I think (when) writing McKay, they wanted to feature someone who’s really fallen in their life and struggled to get back up,” Dourif says. “(She’s) had addiction problems, been arrested, just struggled in ways that a lot of doctors who went to a good school and then medical school and then residency and then attending don’t have exposure to.”

Below, TODAY.com caught up with Dourif to reflect on Season 2, her thoughts ahead of the Sept. 14 Emmy Awards and get as much as possible out of her about the highly anticipated Season 3 of “The Pitt,” due to return in January.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity.
We’re on Episode 5 now. So I have a full-time Monday through Friday job. I report in.
“No matter how bad it gets in the hospital, it will never be as bad as where she’s been.”
Everybody has their story, but it took me longer to get my feet on the ground. I had some sad things happen to my family, and I think I just had that quality, whatever it was.

I got two paragraphs in the character breakdown for the initial audition. I remember reading it and saying to myself, “If they’re going for somebody who looks like me, I’m a version of the character.” I knew right away. And mind you, the audition scenes were mostly medicine. It was very little about me ... but it was mostly just a vibe. I think they were really looking for the essence of the person.

And then when we were cast, I was brought into this room with (executive producer) John Wells and (creator) Scott Gemmill, and they said, “Here’s what we’ve written about McKay’s backstory. You can take or leave whatever you want. This was just our idea of it,” and they read it through. There’s some things that are quite different from me. There’s a lot that’s pretty similar to my actual life.
They are nimble with what we fill in and where we take it, the character. But I’ve never played something so close to Fiona. It’s quite vulnerable to be honest.

Something to do with McKay’s relationship with her mother that was sort of alluded to didn’t resonate with me, and that I don’t really think about. Oftentimes when I’m preparing a scene or a character, I figure out what activates me, and it doesn’t necessarily have to be close to me.

I’m often figuring out what sort of gestalt events led to the conditioning to make the character react a certain way in a scene, which is kind of the puzzle and the joy of acting. It’s one of my favorite parts.
But yeah, there’s some stuff that worked for them that doesn’t work for me. I left that vague.

I think a lot of times in life and in relationships, a secret is much more powerful than something said out loud, and you feel it. And so, oftentimes, I have worked in a secret and if I say it out loud or I tell the other people in the room, it dissipates it. So that’s something I’ve been playing with since the beginning of acting. I worked with Peter Facinelli, I don’t know if you know him from “Twilight,” but he used to tell me that his secret was, every day was his character’s birthday.
So it was just this sort of added quality to everything that I thought was really interesting.
Nobody knows it.

The most enjoyable part, really, is figuring out why these things are happening. You have to let go of everything while you’re actually performing, or it can become kind of heady and controlled. It’s interweaving meaning and interest and all of that stuff. It’s like this psychological puzzle I really like playing with.
I certainly want to turn my brain off. When we’re shooting, I get home at 7:30 (p.m.). If I’m up at 6 (a.m.), you can’t really even turn a screen on if you want to be tired by 9:30 (p.m.).

So I often just sit on my couch. There’s no music. There’s no stimulus. There’s no book. I’m just sitting there, and then I’ll wake up. I’ll sit outside. I’ll have some tea. I talk to a friend on FaceTime. Go over my lines and go to sleep. I’m reading a book on Lojong.

I was trying to describe this to a friend the other day. When I’m on set for “The Pitt,” especially now in Season 3, I feel like I’m 12 years old. Because we’ve all been working together for so long, and also the season is so long. It’s like seven and a half months (of filming). It’s just become this playful, medical camp. I get very silly. It’s really fun.
It feels good. I feel like I’m on a roller coaster. I’m 44. I appreciate every moment of it. I wasn’t expecting it. It’s delightful. It’s ephemeral. I feel like the luckiest girl in the world.
One thing that’s very cool about “The Pitt” actually is it’s very much treated like work. I think there was negotiations to have a shoot on the day of the actual Emmys.

You arrive on time. You are professional. You don’t have people running around catering to you. We don’t have special chairs. We don’t have any of that. We’re there to work along with everybody else that’s there to work. We’re all in scrubs, even the crew, too. And it feels very much like this unit that’s coming together to make the show, which is one of the reasons why the awards are very fun, but they kind of feel odd to pick some pieces out because none of it would work if it wasn’t all of us.

There were a few things that happened (at) the end of my mother’s life where I stepped into a caretaking role for many years before she finally passed in 2015, that gave me the quality in a very direct way for McKay. It’s the reason why I was right (for the part), without question. I knew that from the jump. I knew it from reading the initial character breakdown.

And my mother really loved hospital shows. My mother would have loved “The Pitt” before she got sick. And a lot of the themes, especially in Season 3, that I’m really working with are part of my mother’s story. It feels like the whole thing is some wild, serendipitous kismet workaround of me honoring her and the grief. It feels good and odd and beautiful, and I feel very lucky.
If there’s some kind of afterlife, I hope she’s watching. She would have been so proud of me. She would have told everybody.

title: Melissa Joan Hart’s Movie Premiere Photos Show Why You Shouldn’t Trust Every Picture
summary: Melissa Joan Hart shares two photos from the 2013 “Frozen” premiere, showing how lighting, angles and expressions can change how we see our bodies.
story: Melissa Joan Hart has spent most of her life being photographed.

A former child star, she knows something about how much a single snapshot can shape the way we see someone: A camera can make a moment look polished, awkward, glamorous or unflattering, sometimes within the span of a few seconds.
Recently, Hart offered a particularly good example.

She shared on Instagram two photographs of herself from the 2013 premiere of “Frozen.” In one, she is standing on the red carpet in a fitted blue dress, smiling while facing the camera with her arm on her hip. In the other, she is caught from the side, apparently unaware she is being photographed.
“The difference a little lighting, camera angle, and facial expression can make,” Hart wrote in the caption, adding the hashtags #smokeandmirrors and #professionalphotographer vs. #reallife.
The post struck a chord, and many of the comments zeroed in on something bigger than a celebrity looking different from one photograph to the next.
“I wish we could post this everywhere. This is what we need to normalize. Especially for women and girls. Thank you,” one commenter wrote.
“Melissa this is so important for women to see, thank you! You are so beautiful,” another added.

Hart, who grew up on television, first as the star of “Clarissa Explains It All” and later “Sabrina the Teenage Witch,” has been candid about the pressure that can come with that scrutiny, particularly as women get older. Now 50 and a mother to three sons , Mason, 20, Braydon, 18, and Tucker, 13, she has spent much of her adult life navigating that scrutiny in the public eye.
In a 2019 interview with Us Weekly, Hart acknowledged that maintaining a certain weight can be difficult in an industry where actresses are constantly being photographed and judged.
